topic.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topic.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings
evidence: Solve 'There are 6 apples, 2 are eaten, how many left?' using counters
Solve 'add to' and 'take from' result-unknown problems
Solve 'put together/take apart' problems with total unknown
topic.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'There are 7 birds on a fence and 3 fly away — how many are left?', can {{name}} work it out using their fingers, counters, or a quick drawing?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Solve addition and subtraction WORD PROBLEMS within 10 using objects or drawings — applying the combining/taking-away concepts to real situations by modelling them concretely.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.2 'solve addition and subtraction word problems, and add and subtract within 10… by using objects or drawings'; the CGI problem taxonomy (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare — with the unknown in various positions) frames difficulty.
• Operational details — The core skill is MODELLING: read/hear the situation, represent it with objects or a drawing, then read the answer off the model. Vary the problem STRUCTURE (result-unknown is easiest; change-unknown and start-unknown are harder) and the unknown POSITION, not just the numbers. Discourage keyword-matching ('altogether = add'); instead have children act out or draw what is happening. Keep totals within 10 so the count is manageable.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): solve a result-unknown add-to or take-from story with counters. Tier B (age 5): choose objects/drawing to model a put-together or take-apart problem and state the answer. Tier C (age 5-6): model a change-unknown or simple compare problem and explain how the drawing matches the story.
bestPractices: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: children act out or draw the SITUATION and read the answer from it, so 'altogether'/'left' don't become false triggers for +/−.
Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown; compare) so children build a robust sense of the operations, not one rote pattern.
Use consistent representations (counters, part-whole, bar/tape) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.
Have children retell the problem in their own words and point to each quantity in their model, tying language to representation to answer.
Start with result-unknown, keep numbers within 10, and introduce missing-number/compare forms only once modelling of simple problems is secure.
keyRepresentations: Counters/cubes acted on to match the story
Children's drawings/jottings (dots, crossing-out) of the situation
Part-part-whole model mapping story quantities to parts and whole
Simple bar/tape model for compare problems ('how many more')
Five-frame/ten-frame to organise the objects being combined or removed
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching ('altogether'→add, 'left'→subtract) instead of modelling the situation, which fails on compare and change/start-unknown problems.
Modelling only result-unknown structures and being stuck when the unknown is the change or the start.
Grabbing the two numbers in the problem and combining them regardless of what the story describes.
Miscounting the objects when acting out, or not matching the drawing to the actual quantities in the story.
For compare problems, adding the two amounts instead of finding the difference.

learn.summary: Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): solve one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 10 by MODELLING the situation with objects or drawings, then reading the answer off the model. The core skill is representing what the story describes (things arriving, leaving, two groups combined, two groups compared, or a mystery start), not keyword-matching. Systematically vary problem structure and unknown position; keep totals within 10 so counting stays manageable.

activities.title: Story-modelling with counters and a mat
feedback: Check that the model matches the STORY, not just that the number is right: ask 'show me with the counters what happens to the apples.'
If the child combines both numbers (answers 8 for the apples, i.e. 6+2), have them act the take-away story out step by step with counters before counting, tying it to the removing action.
For the joining story, ask 'did the number get bigger or smaller — why?' to connect the action to the operation.
If the set-up is correct but the count slips, scaffold one-to-one counting; the modelling is sound, so do not reteach it.
activities.rationale: At this age, word-problem solving IS modelling: reading/hearing the situation, representing it concretely, and reading the result off the representation. Acting out the situation avoids the keyword-matching that fails on harder structures.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
K.OA.2: solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings.
Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
learnerActions: Listen to or look at a short situation, e.g. 'There are 6 apples on the tree; the wind blows 2 down.'
Take 6 apple counters and place them on a mat to match the start of the story.
Act out what happens — move the 2 fallen apples to the ground, or cross them out on a drawing.
Count what is left on the tree and say the answer aloud (4).
Retell the story in your own words and point to each quantity (the 6, the 2, what's left) in your model.
Repeat with a joining story, e.g. 'Sam has 3 marbles and gets 4 more — how many now?', adding counters to match and reading off the total (7).
activities.intendedInsight: You don't need a rule to decide 'add' or 'subtract' — you build what actually happened in the story with objects, and the answer is simply what you can then see and count.

activities.title: Part-whole and compare: beyond result-unknown
feedback: If the child adds the two numbers for the part-unknown (4 + 7 = 11), build the whole (7) and the known part (4) with counters so the gap becomes visible; use a part-whole or bar layout.
For compare problems, if the child adds the two amounts, line the groups up and point to the extra ones to show the difference is what's being asked.
Ask 'how many altogether, and how many do you already know?' to surface which quantity is missing.
Praise a correct layout even before the count, then support careful counting if needed.
activities.rationale: Difficulty is strongly influenced by situation structure and unknown position (as well as number size); missing-part, change-unknown, start-unknown and compare problems defeat keyword rules and rote result-unknown patterns, so they are introduced and modelled explicitly once simple problems are secure.
sourceClaims: Problem difficulty is governed by situation structure and unknown position (Cognitively Guided Instruction taxonomy); teaching modelling rather than keyword-matching improves problem solving.
Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems, including missing-number problems, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Model a put-together problem with a missing part, e.g. 'There are 4 red counters and some blue ones, 7 altogether — how many are blue?'
Build the whole (7) and lay out the known part (4) using a part-part-whole frame.
Find the gap — the blue counters needed to fill the whole — and count them to give the answer (3).
Model a simple compare problem, e.g. 'how many more', by lining up two groups side by side (a bar/tape layout) and finding the difference.
For each problem, say whether it is a putting-together story or a comparing story, and explain how your drawing matches the words.
activities.intendedInsight: When the unknown is a part or a difference, you still build the situation — lay out what you know and find what's missing — rather than just combining the two numbers you can see.

activities.title: Narrate and show (talk alongside the model)
feedback: Prompt the child to connect language to representation: 'show me the part where things leave.'
If narration drifts from the model, pause and re-anchor each spoken quantity to a group of objects.

Keep the talk tied to acting on objects: the age-appropriate expectation is work with concrete objects and pictorial representations, so narration is intended to accompany modelling rather than replace it.
activities.rationale: Retelling the problem and pointing to each quantity ties language to representation to answer. Dialogue can develop sense-making; because the curriculum for this age expects work with concrete objects and drawings, talk is intended to accompany acting on objects, and its standalone efficacy is not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Tell an adult or peer what is happening in the story in your own words.
As you narrate, show each step on the objects or drawing ('first there were six… then two fell…').
Answer prompts such as 'which part do you already know?' and 'what are we trying to find?' while pointing to the model.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the story into your own words and linking each phrase to a quantity in your model builds sense-making, so the words guide the action rather than triggering a reflex operation.

constraints: Teach modelling, not keyword-spotting: 'altogether'/'left'/'more' must not become fixed triggers for + or −, because they fail on compare, change-unknown and start-unknown problems.
Keep totals within 10 so counting is manageable; start with result-unknown and introduce missing-number and compare forms only once simple modelling is secure.
Systematically vary problem structure (add-to, take-from, put-together/take-apart, compare) and unknown position (result-, change-, start-unknown), not just the numbers.

A fixed single-story illustration (tap to count, reveal the answer) can anchor one problem's modelling but cannot let the child model varied structures or make their own drawing; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole skill.

Picture-based multiple-choice items can check whether a child recognises/applies the right operation, but a scored recognition format does not itself elicit the child building a model and can be answered by keyword-matching; if used, pair each item with a picture and avoid phrasing answerable by keyword alone.
Use consistent representations (counters/cubes, part-part-whole, bar/tape, five-/ten-frame) so the model itself carries meaning across problems.

Interactive affordances are optional illustrations, not requirements: e.g. dragging objects onto a mat, crossing out, a part-whole/bar frame to organise quantities, narrated scenes, auto-varying the problem type. These make the mechanism concrete but need not all be present.

The legacy row claimed a scored recognition format 'can't develop the modelling process' and that talk alone is a 'weak' route; these are plausible but not established as universal laws by the cited sources. They have been narrowed to observable affordances / curriculum-grounded qualifications with 'may'/'intended' framing.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing ('no spatial dimension to exploit'); this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been dropped rather than asserted. Physical manipulatives (counters/cubes) remain central and are themselves tactile.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 6 apples, 2 eaten → 4 left; (2) 3 marbles + 4 → 7; (3) 4 red, 7 total → 3 blue. All correct. The error trace 'answers 8 for the apples' corresponds to 6+2 (combining regardless of story) and 'answers 11' corresponds to 4+7 (adding instead of finding the missing part) — both coherent misconception traces, retained as feedback cues.
Internal prerequisite/reteach reference codes from the original row were not migrated into learner-facing content.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Addition as combining or putting together two
topic.description: Understand addition as combining or putting together two groups to find the total
evidence: Model 'putting together' with physical objects and say the total
Act out an 'add to' situation (e.g. 3 children arrive, then 2 more join)
Explain that addition means finding how many altogether
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 4 toy cars and a friend brings 3 more, do they understand that adding means combining both groups — and can they tell you there are now 7 cars altogether?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Understand ADDITION as combining or putting together two groups to find the total ('how many altogether'). One of the two conceptual roots of the whole domain (centrality 0.54) — every later strategy, fact, and algorithm rests on it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving addition (+)…'; 'solve one-step problems that involve addition… using concrete objects and pictorial representations'; non-statutory: 'this establishes addition and subtraction as related operations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 'represent addition… with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings…'; K.OA.2 solve add-to and put-together word problems; the two problem structures (add-to / put-together) are the canonical starting semantics.
• Operational details — Distinguish the two situations under 'combining': ADD-TO (a set grows: 3 here, 2 MORE arrive) and PUT-TOGETHER (two static parts seen as one whole). Model with physical objects the child physically pushes together, narrate the action, then attach the total. Cardinality (last-number-said = how many) is the hard prerequisite — the child must trust the count of the whole. Keep numbers within 5-10 and keep the ACTION visible before any symbol.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): physically combine two groups and re-count all to say the total. Tier B (age 5): act out an add-to story and state 'how many altogether' without prompting to recount from 1. Tier C (age 5-6): explain in words that addition means putting together to find the total, and match a combining situation to the idea of 'more/altogether'.
bestPractices: Teach BOTH combining semantics explicitly — add-to (dynamic: a group grows) and put-together (static: two parts, one whole) — because children who only meet 'and then more came' struggle with part-part-whole and missing-part problems later.
Move through concrete → pictorial → spoken before any + symbol: children push real objects together, then draw, then describe; the symbol (a separate topic) comes only once the ACTION is understood.
Narrate the action and the result separately ('3 and 2 more… that's 5 altogether') so 'altogether/total' becomes attached to the combined quantity, not just the last object counted.
Use fingers, ten-frames and story contexts children act out, so addition is a thing you DO to quantities, not a written procedure to memorise.
Build on secure cardinality: if a child recounts the whole from 1 every time, that is expected early — encourage but do not force 'counting on' until counting-all is fluent.
keyRepresentations: Two groups of physical objects (counters, cubes, toys) that are literally pushed together
Ten-frame(s) filling up as objects are added
Part-part-whole (part-whole 'cherry') model showing two parts joining into a whole
Fingers and five-frames for small totals
Story/act-out situations and simple drawings of an add-to or put-together scene
commonMisconceptions: Recounting the whole from 1 every time and never trusting the total — a cardinality gap surfacing inside addition.
Thinking addition always means 'a group gets bigger by things arriving' (add-to only), so static put-together and part-part-whole situations aren't recognised as addition.
Believing the total is 'the last number you say' regardless of combining, i.e. reciting rather than combining quantities.
Losing track when combining by miscounting the join (double-counting an object or skipping one).
Assuming the bigger group must be said/written first, an early seed of not seeing addition as flexible (commutativity comes later).

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Year 1): understand ADDITION as combining or putting together two groups to find the total ('how many altogether'). Teach both combining meanings explicitly — ADD-TO (a group grows: 3 here, 2 MORE arrive) and PUT-TOGETHER (two static parts seen as one whole). Keep the physical ACTION of joining visible before any written symbol, build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many), and attach the words 'altogether/total' to the whole combined set. Keep numbers small (within 5-10).

activities.title: Combining mat: push two groups into one whole
feedback: If the child names just one group as the total (e.g. says 3): physically push the groups together and count the single combined set with them; contrast 'how many red?' with 'how many altogether?' so the merging is felt. An optional live total counter that climbs 3→4→5 as the piles merge makes the whole-set count visible.

If the child re-counts the whole pile from one every time: this is a normal early stage — do not mark it wrong and do not drill. Keep modelling 'hold 3 in your head... 4, 5' and counting-on emerges as cardinality matures.
If the method is right but the final count slips to 4 or 6: scaffold one-to-one counting by moving each counter aside as it is counted; the combining idea is intact, so do not reteach the concept.
Reinforce by asking the child to re-count the whole and confirm the total is the whole set, not the last object touched.
activities.rationale: Addition-as-combining is an action on quantities; letting the child drag two groups together and watch a single total emerge from their own action is intended to make 'two parts become one countable whole' concrete. Concrete action precedes pictorial and symbolic work, and both add-to and put-together structures are the canonical starting semantics. A live recomputing total and mode toggle are optional supports that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms. This is a proposed activity, not an empirically validated one.

The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.

Y1 pupils read/write/interpret statements involving + and solve one-step addition problems with concrete objects and pictorial representations; addition and subtraction are established as related operations.
learnerActions: Drop three counters into one framed region (a basket or ten-frame) and two counters into a second framed region beside it.
Count each part aloud: 'three red here, two blue here.'
Physically sweep both piles together into a single large 'altogether' region.
Count the whole merged set and say how many there are altogether.
Say the matching sentence aloud: 'three and two more — that's five altogether.' (Leave the written 3 + 2 = 5 for the later, separate symbol topic.)
Switch modes: in ADD-TO, add objects to one existing group one at a time ('3... then 2 more arrive'); in PUT-TOGETHER, start with two ready-made parts and merge them at once.
activities.intendedInsight: Two separate groups the child made become ONE group with a single count — addition felt as a physical join, not a recited fact. 'Altogether' names the whole combined set, however it was built.

activities.title: Act out an add-to story
feedback: If the child only counts the arrivals or only the starting group, replay the story slowly and count everyone present at the end together.
Praise retelling that keeps the action ('and then more came') and the result ('altogether') distinct.
activities.rationale: Children who only meet 'and then more came' can struggle with part-part-whole later, and children who only meet static parts may not recognise growth as addition; acting out add-to stories is intended to secure the dynamic meaning. Story contexts children act out are intended to make addition something the child does to quantities. This is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images and drawings; solve add-to and put-together word problems within 10.
The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.
learnerActions: Act out a situation with real children or toys: e.g. 3 children are on the mat, then 2 more join.
Narrate the action and the result separately: '3 children... then 2 more came... that's 5 altogether.'
State 'how many altogether' after the join without being told to recount from one.
Retell the story using fingers or a five-/ten-frame to show the growing group.
activities.intendedInsight: Add-to situations (a group grows as more arrive) are a form of addition, and the total names the whole group after the new members join.

activities.title: Part-part-whole picture scene and 'altogether?' flap
feedback: If the child gives a subset (e.g. 3): point to each group in turn, then sweep a hand around the whole scene and count everyone.
Use the part-whole diagram to show both parts belong inside one whole.
activities.rationale: A static scene is a clean anchor for the put-together idea and the word 'altogether', but it shows a finished sum rather than letting the child perform the join — so it labels the act more than it builds it. Use it as a scaffold alongside hands-on combining, not as the sole route.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1/2: represent addition with objects, fingers, mental images and drawings; solve add-to and put-together word problems within 10.
The add-to and put-together situation types are the canonical starting semantics for addition, and concrete-pictorial modelling precedes symbolic work.
learnerActions: Look at a static scene with two groups (e.g. 3 ducks on the bank, 2 ducks in the water).
Count each group by pointing to it.
Answer 'how many altogether?' and then check by lifting a flap or revealing the total.
Fit the two parts into a part-whole ('cherry') diagram: two parts joining into one whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Two static parts can be seen together as one whole — the put-together meaning of addition — even when nothing is moving or arriving.

activities.title: Talk it through while combining
feedback: Accept gestures and object-moves as valid explanations at this age; the child's language is still forming.

If the child insists the bigger group must come first, let them combine in both orders and count — they should find the same total (an informal, early seed of commutativity, which is formalised later).
activities.rationale: Dialogue can elicit a young child's thinking and may reveal whether they treat two groups as one total, but the concept is fundamentally about acting on objects, so talk should sit alongside manipulables rather than replace them. Noticing order-independence here is an early, informal seed (formal commutativity comes later).
learnerActions: Alongside real objects, respond to a warm prompt: 'Let's put these together — how many now?'
Explain in words what 'altogether' means by showing it with the counters.
Answer probing questions: 'If I add the blue ones to the red ones instead of red to blue, do we still get 5? Why?' and 'What if there were 3 red and 4 blue — how many altogether?'
If a pretend friend says the answer is 3, explain what you would tell them.
activities.intendedInsight: A child can articulate that addition means combining to find how many altogether, and begins to notice the order of combining doesn't change the total.

constraints: Keep numbers within 5-10 and keep the joining action visible before introducing the + symbol; the written symbol is a later, separate topic.
Build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many). If the child cannot trust the count of the whole, that prerequisite needs attention before counting-on is expected.
Counting-all from one is an expected early developmental stage — encourage but do not force 'counting on', and do not mark counting-all as wrong.
Picture-only scenes and lift-the-flap totals are scaffolds for the 'altogether' label; they do not let the child perform the combining and should not be the only experience.

A scored multiple-choice/linear check may test recognition of a combined total but does not itself elicit the child's physical combining or spoken explanation, and such assessment is developmentally weak at ages 4-6; keep any such check to picture-based items with very small numbers and never as the main activity.

On-screen 3D manipulation (rotating or positioning virtual 3D objects) adds handling cost for pre-readers without a clear conceptual gain here (combining small groups has little spatial payoff), so flat on-screen objects/scenes and real physical counters are preferred for this topic; this is a scoped judgement, not a claim that 3D never helps.
Teach both add-to and put-together explicitly so children recognise static part-part-whole situations as addition too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M and NCETM claims are marked unverified. Do not treat citations as evidence that these specific activities were tested.

The source's stated correct answer prefers 'counting on from the larger group', while its own guidance says counting-all is normal and should not be drilled at this age. These are consistent if 'counting on' is treated as the maturing goal, not the required method for ages 4-6; activities present counting-all as acceptable and counting-on as emerging.
The 'live total counter', mode toggle, drag-and-sweep, and lift-the-flap are retained as optional interaction/feedback examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not mandatory mechanisms.

The original pedagogy listed age-tiered Checkpoint expectations (Tier A ~age 4: combine and re-count all; Tier B ~age 5: act out an add-to story and state 'altogether' without prompting to recount; Tier C ~age 5-6: explain in words that addition means putting together). These are distributed across the three activities here rather than presented as explicit age-banded milestones; reconstruct the tier mapping if age-specific checks are needed.

probeDeeper: If I add the blue ones to the red ones instead of red to blue, do we still get 5? Why?
What if there were 3 red and 4 blue — how many altogether?
Show me with the counters what 'altogether' means.
A friend says the answer is 3. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: 5 — found by combining the two groups into one, ideally counting ON from the larger group ('3 … 4, 5') or just knowing 3 and 2 make 5, rather than recounting every counter from one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts ALL from one every time — cannot hold the first quantity and count on, so recounts the whole merged pile from 1.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill counting-on or mark counting-all as wrong — it is a normal developmental stage that matures with cardinality; keep modelling 'hold 3 in your head, count on' and it emerges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child re-counts every counter from one rather than counting on from 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names one visible group as the total — answers 3 (or 2), treating 'altogether' as relabelling a group rather than merging both.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically push the groups together and count the single combined set; contrast 'how many red' with 'how many altogether' so combining is felt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives a subset count (3 or 2) as the total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Combines correctly but miscounts the merged pile (double-counts or skips a counter).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold one-to-one by moving each counter as it is counted; the combining concept is intact, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method is right (counts on / merges) but the final count slips to 4 or 6.

responseLevels.gap: Names one group as the total, or cannot find the total without recounting from one and still errs.
responseLevels.full: Treats the two groups as one total, counts on from the larger or recalls the fact, and explains that combining finds how many altogether.
responseLevels.partial: Finds 5 reliably but only by counting all from one; does not yet count on or recall, and combining is procedure-bound.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. If I put them together, how many are there altogether? How did you work it out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The number 5 alone does not reveal understanding; the METHOD and reason do. A child who grasps addition as combining treats the two groups as one merged total and counts on or recalls; a child who does not may name one of the groups as the answer, or must always recount the whole set from one. Asking 'how did you work it out' exposes which.

• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), REPRESENTATIONAL. Children externalise a calculation so they can reason about and communicate it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): solve problems 'using concrete objects and pictorial representations'; the concrete–pictorial–abstract progression is the backbone of KS1 additive work.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 'represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings…, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations'.
• Operational details — Deliberately cycle the SAME calculation through multiple representations — real objects → drawing → finger/mental image → spoken → number sentence — and ask the child to connect them ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'). Use consistent structured models (ten-frames, part-whole, fingers) so representations accumulate meaning rather than being ad hoc each time.
Have children narrate their representation aloud ('I drew 5 and crossed out 2') to tie drawing to action to language.
Value the child's own drawings/jottings while nudging toward clearer, more mathematical ones (dots/marks over detailed pictures) to keep focus on quantity.

topic.description: Understand subtraction as taking away or separating from a group to find how many remain

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Understand SUBTRACTION as taking away / separating from a group to find how many remain. The single most central node in the domain (centrality 0.65) — partner concept to addition-as-combining and the root of all later subtraction work.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving… subtraction (−)…'; 'solve one-step problems that involve… subtraction, using concrete objects and pictorial representations, and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1/2 represent subtraction and solve take-from problems within 10; take-from (result unknown) is the canonical entry semantics.
• Operational details — Introduce take-away/separate first (remove objects, count what's left), but flag early that subtraction ALSO answers 'how many more/difference' and 'missing part' — these comparison and unknown-part meanings are where children later struggle if only 'take away' is taught. Model the physical removal, narrate it, then count the remainder. Keep within 5-10 with objects the child physically removes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): physically remove some objects and count how many remain. Tier B (age 5): act out a take-from story ('5 biscuits, eat 2') and say how many are left. Tier C (age 5-6): explain subtraction as finding what's left, and recognise a simple 'how many more' difference situation as also being subtraction.
bestPractices: Start with take-away/separate (physically remove and count the remainder) because it is the most concrete meaning, but do NOT stop there — deliberately introduce comparison ('how many more') and missing-part meanings so subtraction isn't permanently equated with 'take away'.
Keep the removed part visible then hidden: showing what was taken and what remains helps the child see the whole splitting into part-taken and part-left (links to part-part-whole).
Narrate action then result ('5 biscuits, take away 2… 3 are left') so 'how many left/remain' attaches to the remaining quantity.
Use the same manipulatives and stories as addition, then contrast: combining makes more, separating leaves fewer — building addition and subtraction as inverse actions from the very start.
Ground the missing-number form (7 = ? − 9 style, or 5 − ? = 3) in acting out, so subtraction-as-unknown-part has an early concrete seed for later formalisation.

Part-part-whole model: whole splits into part-taken and part-left

Act-out story scenes and drawings with a crossing-out to show removal
commonMisconceptions: Equating subtraction ONLY with 'take away', so comparison ('how many more') and missing-part problems aren't recognised as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.
Trying to 'take away' the larger from the smaller in a comparison and getting confused, or reversing to keep it 'takeable'.
Recounting the whole rather than the remainder, or counting the removed objects instead of what's left.
Believing subtraction always makes a number 'small' and being surprised that 8 − 1 is still large.
Reading 7 − 3 left-to-right as an instruction with no sense that it asks 'how many remain', so missing-number forms feel impossible.

constraints: Keep quantities within 5-10 and use objects the child can physically remove.

Do not stop at 'take away': deliberately introduce comparison (difference) and missing-part meanings. The evidence base identifies that if only 'take away' is taught, children tend to stop recognising comparison and missing-part problems as subtraction — the classic long-run difficulty.

A still take-from picture (crossed-out/bite scene with tap-to-reveal) anchors the take-away meaning but does not let the child perform the removal or explore comparison/missing-part meanings; treat it as a scaffold, not the sole teacher.

Talk-only prompts lean on still-forming language at this age; pair any 'how many are left?' conversation with real objects rather than using it alone. This does not mean talk cannot support reasoning.
Do not insist on counting-back or mark slow recounting of the remainder as wrong; counting-back matures later. Removing objects and recounting the remainder is acceptable.

Scored, linear picture quizzes are developmentally weak for ages 4-6; a small picture item may check recognition of 'how many left' but does not itself elicit the child's own physical removal, so keep any such item minor and not the primary route for building the concept.

Watch for 'subtraction always makes a number small': show that taking away leaves fewer than the start but not necessarily a small amount (e.g. 8 − 1 = 7, still a lot), so the child isn't surprised by it.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6 (UK Y1), learners add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers within 20, including the +0/−0 case, using known number bonds and making-ten rather than counting all. Core aims: fluent within-20 calculation, correct bridging across ten (e.g. 8+7), and understanding that adding or subtracting zero leaves a quantity unchanged. Activities centre on acting out calculations with ten-frames and number lines, with a concrete treatment of the zero case to dispel the belief that every operation must change the number.

activities.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
feedback: If the learner counts all from one, prompt: hold the first number in mind and count on only the second (hold 14, count on 5 more).
For a bridging case, ask how many more are needed to fill the frame to ten, then how many are left over (8 needs 2 more to make ten, leaving 5, so 15).
If the answer is off by one on the number line, have them name the first jump aloud and check they didn't count the starting number itself as a jump (17 − 3: start at 17, jump back 3 to 14).
activities.rationale: Acting out a calculation on a ten-frame and number line keeps the procedure tied to meaning and reinforces the making-ten strategy at the teen boundary, where ones-counting is error-prone. A live, re-drivable calculation where counters move and a number sentence forms makes the strategy visible; a fixed worked example cannot be re-driven with new numbers.
sourceClaims: Explicit concrete treatment of the +0/−0 case dispels the common belief that every operation must change the number; bridging-ten cases need making-ten not ones-counting.
learnerActions: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
activities.intendedInsight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

activities.title: Add nothing, take nothing: the zero case
feedback: If the learner changes the number (e.g. 12 + 0 = 13), act out physically putting zero more counters on, then recount to show the quantity is the same.
Ask directly: when you added nothing, did any counter move? So what is the answer?
Reinforce the contrast: taking 3 away changes the number, taking 0 away does not.
activities.rationale: Young children often assume every operation must change the number, producing errors like 5+0=6 or 5−0=4. Concretely acting out 'add nothing / take nothing' and seeing the quantity unchanged targets this directly and establishes zero's identity role. A side-by-side contrast with a non-zero operation sharpens the point.

learnerActions: Build a number on a double ten-frame (e.g. 12: one full frame and 2 on the second frame).
Choose 'add 0' and watch that no counters move and the number stays 12.
Choose 'subtract 0' from another number (e.g. 16) and confirm it stays 16.
Show the same on the number line as a jump of length zero that stays on the spot.
Say or write why the number did not change: adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity exactly as it was.
Contrast with a nearby case that does change (17 − 3 vs 17 − 0).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged (n + 0 = n, n − 0 = n); not every operation changes the quantity.

activities.title: Spoken probe: what happens if we add zero?
feedback: If the explanation is 'it just stays', press for why: because no amount was added or taken away.
Accept correct reasoning expressed in the child's own words; follow a wrong prediction by acting it out with objects.
activities.rationale: A short dialogue may surface the identity idea and let the child articulate reasoning, which the top checkpoint tier expects. Discussion complements, but is not itself calculation practice; the hands-on activities remain the vehicle for building and rehearsing the procedure. Efficacy of the dialogue as a standalone is proposed, not evidenced.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?'
Explain in your own words how 17 − 3 is different from 17 − 0.
Predict and justify the answer to a new zero case before checking it with objects.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state why adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged shows understanding beyond getting the answer.

activities.title: Mixed within-20 practice set
feedback: For an answer like 14 + 5 = 64, show that the 5 ones are added to the 4 ones, not to the ten; make place value visible with tens-and-ones.
For a changed zero answer, re-act adding/taking nothing.
For an off-by-one slip with a sound method, scaffold the count aloud rather than reteaching the strategy.
activities.rationale: Varied practice is needed to build procedural fluency and to probe specific errors (the zero misconception, adding to the wrong part, crossing-ten slips). Including missing-number items lightly connects to later algebraic work. A practice set drills the procedure but relies on the making-ten strategy having been built elsewhere (for example, in the hands-on calculator activity); it does not by itself teach that strategy.

learnerActions: Work a varied set spanning non-bridging sums (14 + 5), bridging sums (8 + 7), take-aways (17 − 3, 15 − 7), and several +0/−0 items (12 + 0, 16 − 0).
Occasionally solve a missing-number item (e.g. 14 + ? = 19) to vary which quantity is unknown.
Jot a number line or ten-frame when helpful.

For non-bridging items, say which digit changed and which stayed the same (14 + 5 → the ones change, 4 + 5 = 9 → 19); notice that in bridging items like 8 + 7 the tens change too, and in ±0 items no digit changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency comes from applying bonds and making-ten across the full 0-20 range, including the zero cases and the teen boundary.

constraints: Keep calculations within the 0-20 range, including the teen boundary (crossing ten).

A practice set drills and assesses the procedure but does not by itself build the making-ten strategy; discussion surfaces reasoning but is not calculation practice. The hands-on calculation is the proposed primary vehicle for building the strategy here, with efficacy stated as proposed rather than proven.

Tiered expectations: at age 5, non-bridging cases via a fast strategy; age 5-6, bridging cases and correct +0/−0; age 6, fluent within-20 calculation with an explanation of why ±0 leaves the number unchanged.

Distinguish subtraction meaning when ordering: 17 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 17; do not reorder subtraction to keep the larger number first without noting the meaning changes (and 3 − 17 lies outside the Y1 within-20 range).

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2). Solve one-step WORD PROBLEMS involving addition and subtraction to 20, INCLUDING missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9). Extends within-10 modelling to a larger range and, importantly, to problems where the unknown is not the result.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction… and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.1 'use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems… with unknowns in all positions'; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
• Operational details — Continue modelling the SITUATION (act out / draw / bar model) rather than keyword-matching, now with numbers to 20 and with the unknown in the start, change or result position. Missing-number problems are the key new demand: the child must represent an unknown and reason to it, often using the inverse or a known bond. Bar/part-whole models become powerful here for making the unknown visible.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): solve result-unknown add/subtract problems to 20 by modelling. Tier B (age 6): solve change-unknown problems and simple missing-number equations with support. Tier C (age 6-7): solve start-unknown and missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9), explaining the model and using the inverse to find the unknown.
bestPractices: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending to numbers to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible so children can reason to it.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and to known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children write the equation that matches the situation, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after =).
Progress difficulty by problem structure, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
keyRepresentations: Bar/tape model showing known parts and an unknown
Part-part-whole model with the unknown in any slot
Objects/drawings acted on to match the story
Empty number line for counting on to find a difference/unknown
Equations with a box/letter for the unknown in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching (fails on missing-number and compare problems).
Assuming the unknown is always the result, so start- and change-unknown problems stump them.
Rejecting missing-number forms because = is read as 'answer here'.
Combining the two given numbers regardless of the structure (e.g. adding in a start-unknown problem that needs subtraction).
Not using the inverse/known bond to find the unknown, instead guessing.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2): solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9. The core objective is modelling the situation (acting out, drawing, bar/part-whole models) rather than keyword-matching, and crucially handling problems where the unknown sits in the start, change or result position — not only the answer slot. Bar/part-whole models make the unknown visible so children can reason to it using the inverse or a known bond.

activities.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
feedback: Check the structure of the model, not just the final number: does the bar place the known parts and the unknown where the story puts them?

If the pieces dragged in don't match the story — for example a given whole treated as a part, or both numbers entered as parts when one of them is actually the whole — ask them to re-read it event by event: 'What was there to begin with? What happened? What is left?'
For 7 = ? − 9, prompt: 'We start with a mystery number, take away 9, and 7 are left — so the mystery number is 9 and 7 put together, 16.'

Praise correctly reasoning to an unknown via the inverse or a known bond, and show how the model did the work: adding the parts to find a missing whole, or taking a known part from the whole to find a missing part.
activities.rationale: The skill is modelling situations with the unknown in varied positions; a build-your-own bar/part-whole model lets the child place the unknown and manipulate it so the inverse is made visible, with varied problem structures generated across a session. An interactive model can rotate the unknown position and give feedback on the structure of the model, which a fixed worked example cannot do, though a fixed example can still illustrate the method. Proposed design; efficacy not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
activities.intendedInsight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

activities.title: Hands-on modelling with counters, drawings and paper bars
feedback: If the model and story disagree, re-read the story one event at a time and adjust the counters/bar.
Reinforce that 'took away / left' does not automatically mean subtract — the structure of the story decides the operation.
Celebrate explanations that justify the operation from the situation, not from a single word.
activities.rationale: Concrete acting-out and drawing underpin the pictorial bar model and give young children a tangible way to represent an unknown before abstract equations. This supports the standards' call for concrete objects and pictorial representations.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Act out or draw the story with physical counters before choosing any operation.
Lay out a paper tape/bar strip and partition it into known parts and an unknown part to match the story.
Use an empty number line to count on and find a difference or an unknown.
Say aloud what you know, what you are trying to find, and why the operation you chose fits the story.
activities.intendedInsight: Modelling the situation with concrete materials — rather than matching keywords — reveals the correct operation even when the unknown is not the result.

activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'
feedback: When a child applies an operation to the two given numbers automatically, without checking the story (e.g. trying 7 − 9 or 9 − 7 for 7 = ? − 9), redirect to the story structure with a question rather than giving the answer.
Follow the child's approach and ask for justification; adapt prompts to whether they are stuck on parsing '=' or on choosing the operation.
activities.rationale: Missing-number and start-unknown problems demand reasoning to an unknown; a Socratic dialogue may develop that reasoning by adapting to the child's approach. Dialogue complements, and does not replace, hands-on and pictorial modelling. This medium's efficacy is a proposal, not verified.
learnerActions: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.

activities.title: Worked bar-model example with revealable steps
feedback: Prompt the learner to predict each next step before revealing it.
Ask them to point to where the unknown sits before the final number is shown.
activities.rationale: A static worked example anchors the pictorial modelling method and can be revisited; it cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem, so it works best as a scaffold before or alongside the interactive builder.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Study one worked problem shown with a bar model.
Reveal the solution steps one at a time and relate each step to the story.
Restate how the parts and whole map onto what the story gave and what it asked.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly worked bar model anchors the method and shows how the unknown is found from the known quantities: combining the parts when the whole is unknown, or taking a known part from the whole when a part is unknown.

activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
feedback: If a child answers 7 = ▢ − 9 as 7 − 9 or refuses, return to the bar model: whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 16.

If a child subtracts on a take-away start-unknown problem (e.g. 'I had some, ate 9, 7 are left'), have them act it out to see that the start was larger than what remained. (On an add-on start-unknown problem such as 'I had some, got 5 more, now I have 12', subtracting 12 − 5 is correct.)
activities.rationale: Varied-position items probe the target directly and surface misconceptions, but practice/fill-in tasks present problems to solve and may not by themselves build the modelling process, so they belong after modelling work rather than before it.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
learnerActions: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.intendedInsight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.

Practice/fill-in items probe the target and surface misconceptions but do not by themselves build the modelling process; use them after hands-on and pictorial modelling.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1), LANGUAGE. Read, write and interpret the symbols +, − and = in number sentences — attaching formal notation to the already-understood actions of combining and taking away. A highly central bridging node (centrality 0.38): notation unlocks recording, communicating and later manipulating calculations.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving addition (+), subtraction (−) and equals (=) signs'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 use expressions/equations; 1.OA.7 'understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations… are true or false' (the deeper = meaning is a later dependent, mt_oIzycTBeE4).
• Operational details — Introduce each symbol as a written record of an action the child already does: + records combining, − records taking away, = records 'is the same as / results in'. Read sentences aloud in full ('three plus two equals five') and write sentences to match concrete situations (both directions). Critically, model = as balance/'same as' from the outset (present 5 = 3 + 2 and 3 + 2 = 2 + 3, not only left-to-right 'answer' forms) to pre-empt the operator misconception.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): read 3 + 2 = 5 aloud correctly and point to each symbol's meaning. Tier B (age 5-6): write a number sentence to match a concrete add or subtract situation. Tier C (age 6): recognise = as 'is the same as' by accepting 5 = 3 + 2 and judging a simple sentence true/false.
bestPractices: Attach each symbol to an action the child already performs — + to combining, − to removing, = to 'is the same as' — rather than teaching symbols as abstract marks to decode.
From the very first lessons present = in varied positions (5 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2), never only 'sum then answer', to stop = being learned as 'write the answer here'.
Practise both directions: read a symbolic sentence and act it out; and write a sentence to match a concrete/pictorial situation.
Read sentences aloud in full mathematical language ('plus', 'minus/subtract', 'equals / is the same as') so notation and vocabulary co-develop.
Keep the referent quantities visible (objects/ten-frame beside the sentence) so symbols stay tied to meaning, not just to each other.
keyRepresentations: The three symbol cards +, −, = alongside the concrete action each records
Number sentences built from digit + symbol cards under a concrete model
Ten-frame / part-whole model paired with its matching equation
A simple two-pan balance image for = as 'same value on both sides'
True/false sentence cards for interrogating the = meaning
commonMisconceptions: Reading = as 'the answer comes next' (an operator/'makes') rather than 'is the same as', so 5 = 3 + 2 or 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 look wrong.
Confusing + and − by shape/name, especially when reading quickly, or ignoring the symbol and just combining whatever numbers appear.
Writing sentences with the operation and answer in the wrong order, or omitting the = sign.
Treating the number sentence as a left-to-right instruction to 'do something' with no sense that it states a relationship.
Believing something must always be written after the = (rejecting 7 = 3 + 4 or missing-number forms).

learn.summary: Ages 5-6 (Y1) language/notation goal: read, write and interpret the symbols +, − and = in number sentences, attaching formal notation to the already-understood actions of combining and taking away. The central design move is to introduce = relationally ('is the same as') from the very start, presenting it in varied positions (5 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3) to pre-empt the common 'the answer comes next' operator misconception. Activities below span a hands-on sentence-builder with a balance, symbol-and-action reference work, notation practice, and a short probing dialogue — each with a distinct pedagogical purpose.

activities.title: Sentence builder linked to a balance
feedback: If the child reads = as 'the answer is', show 5 = 3 + 2 on the balance: the sides are equal, so the sentence is true even with the total first; use 'is the same as' language.
If the child builds a sentence the balance won't level for, ask them to count both sides and compare — the tipping beam shows the two sides are not the same value.
When they accept 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 as true, name the discovery: '= means same as, so both sides can be sums.'
activities.rationale: Letting the symbol appear as a record of an action, and using a balance to enforce 'same value both sides', ties notation to meaning and is intended to address the operator-equals misconception. OPTIONAL interactive affordances (auto-inserting the matching symbol when counters are combined/removed, a beam that tips unless sides match, draggable number/symbol cards) can make the mechanism concrete; a physical two-pan balance with counters is an equally valid medium. These are example mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving +, − and = signs.
Presenting the equals sign in varied (non-canonical) positions from the start counters the pervasive operator/'makes' misconception.
1.OA.7: understand the meaning of the equal sign and determine whether equations are true or false (e.g. 6 = 6, 7 = 8 − 1).
learnerActions: Push two groups of counters together on a work surface and record what happened with a sentence strip, placing a '+' between the groups; take some counters away and use a '−' instead.

Build the sentence 3 + 2 = 5 and check the two sides balance (a two-pan balance loaded with identical counters or cubes, so that weight goes up with count, or a balance image/animation that only levels when both sides have the same value).
Now build 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 and notice the sides STILL balance — discuss why this is allowed even though no single 'answer' sits after the =.
Try true/false sentences (e.g. 5 = 3 + 2 (true), 4 + 1 = 3 + 2 (true, both equal 5), 3 + 2 = 2 + 1 (false)) and predict whether the balance will level or tip before testing.
Keep the referent objects (counters / ten-frame / part-whole model) visible beside the sentence throughout.
activities.intendedInsight: The symbols record actions the child already does (+ = combining, − = taking away) and = means 'the same value on both sides', not 'write the answer here' — so numbers may legitimately appear on either side.

activities.title: Both directions: read-and-act, then write-to-match
feedback: If the child omits the = or writes a sentence that does not match the situation (e.g. 2 − 5 for taking 2 away from 5), point back to the acted-out situation and ask which part of the sentence shows each step; remember that answer-first forms such as 5 = 3 + 2 are correct, not a wrong order.
If a child reads − as 'and' or acts out combining for a minus, re-pair the symbol with the removing action in context and re-read.
Reversed or mirror-written digits/symbols at this age are a normal early-writing stage, not a maths error: model correct orientation and move on; do not drill-correct as a misunderstanding.
activities.rationale: Practising both directions (symbol→action and situation→symbol) and reading aloud in full keeps symbols attached to the actions and vocabulary they name. Keeping referent quantities visible prevents symbols becoming marks related only to each other.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils read, write and interpret mathematical statements involving +, − and = signs.
learnerActions: Read a symbolic sentence aloud in full mathematical language ('three plus two equals five'; 'five minus two is the same as three') and act it out with objects.
Point to each symbol in turn and say what it records: + 'put together', − 'take away', = 'is the same as'.
Watch or hear a concrete/pictorial situation (e.g. three ducks swimming and two more joining) and WRITE a number sentence that matches it, including the = sign.
Write a take-away story of your own and record it with a sentence using the − sign.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a sentence and enacting it, and writing a sentence to capture a real situation, are two sides of the same skill: notation and spoken vocabulary co-develop and stay tied to meaning.

activities.title: Symbol-and-action reference wall
feedback: Direct the child to the matching action card when they confuse + and −.
Remind, via the = card, that 'is the same as' allows numbers on either side.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference supports memory and vocabulary. It cannot let the child build or test sentences, so it complements rather than replaces the sentence builder; use it alongside generative tasks.
learnerActions: Study a reference display showing each symbol beside the action it records, with a lift-the-flap or tap-to-reveal meaning ('plus means put together', 'minus means take away', 'equals means is the same as').
Study one fully worked sentence tied to a concrete model.
Use the wall as a check: when unsure which symbol to write, find the matching action.
activities.intendedInsight: A stable anchor linking each symbol to its meaning and vocabulary supports recall while building and writing sentences.

activities.title: Notation practice: choose and judge
feedback: If a child marks 5 = 3 + 2 false, revisit 'is the same as' with objects or a balance: both sides equal 5.
If +/− are swapped, send the child back to the action behind each symbol.
activities.rationale: Selected-response and true/false items can help consolidate recognition of what each symbol records, and — when = is shown in non-standard positions — can reveal the operator-equals misconception. They assess and reinforce recognition but do not elicit independent construction of a sentence, so they should follow the building and writing work, not stand alone.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.7: understand the meaning of the equal sign and determine whether equations are true or false (e.g. 6 = 6, 7 = 8 − 1).
learnerActions: Choose the symbol that matches a described action (which sign for 'putting together'? for 'taking away'?).
Fill the blank: 3 __ 2 = 5; 4 __ 1 = 3 (choosing + or −).
Match a number sentence to the picture or story it describes.
Judge true/false for = sentences in non-standard positions: 5 = 3 + 2 (true), 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 (true), 4 + 1 = 2 + 2 (false).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recognition of what each symbol records, and relational judgement of = sentences, consolidates the notation and surfaces the operator-equals error.

activities.title: What does this = mean here? (short probe)
feedback: If the child insists something must always follow the =, show 7 = 3 + 4 on a balance or with objects and restate 'is the same as'.
Affirm relational language ('both sides are the same amount') when it appears.
activities.rationale: A focused dialogue can surface and challenge the operator-equals misconception. Here it is used as a short probe tied to a concrete sentence and paired with building and writing practice, since reading/writing symbols is a notational skill that also needs construction work — not as a claim that talk alone is sufficient or superior.
sourceClaims: Presenting the equals sign in varied (non-canonical) positions from the start counters the pervasive operator/'makes' misconception.
learnerActions: Look at a true/false sentence with = in a non-standard position (e.g. 7 = 3 + 4) and explain what the = sign is telling us about the two sides.
Answer: is 5 = 3 + 2 allowed, or must it be 3 + 2 = 5? Say why.
Point to the part of a number sentence that shows a change (e.g. in 3 + 2 = 5 for the duck story, the '+ 2' shows the two more ducks arriving).
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the relational meaning of = makes the child's reading explicit and can expose any residual operator view.

constraints: Present = relationally from the first lessons and in varied positions (5 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2); never only 'sum then answer', which teaches = as 'write the answer here'.
Keep referent quantities (objects/ten-frame/part-whole model) visible beside sentences so symbols stay tied to meaning.
The reference wall is a scaffold: it anchors meaning but cannot let the child build or test sentences, so pair it with generative tasks.
Selected-response and true/false items assess and reinforce recognition but do not elicit independent construction of a sentence; use them after building/writing, not instead of it.
Mirror-writing or reversed digits/symbols at ages 5-6 are a normal early-writing developmental stage, not a maths misconception; model correct orientation rather than drilling it as an error.
Read sentences aloud in full mathematical language ('plus', 'minus/subtract', 'equals / is the same as') so notation and vocabulary co-develop.
The deeper true/false relational understanding of = is a later dependent objective; at this stage aim for accepting non-canonical forms and simple true/false judgements, not full equation reasoning.
Ensure any sentence used to 'balance' has genuinely equal sides (e.g. 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 both equal 5) and any 'false' example has unequal sides (e.g. 4 + 1 = 2 + 2).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row claimed '3D adds nothing' for symbol notation; this universal-necessity framing is not established by the evidence and has been dropped. No 3D activity is proposed because notation is not inherently spatial, but this is a design judgement, not a proven limit.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (CCSS 1.OA.7 and the McNeil/Alibali-NCETM relational-equals claim); treat the relational-equals pedagogy as well-motivated but not independently re-verified here.

Comparative-efficacy wording about dialogue vs building/writing, and efficiency/certainty wording about selected-response items, have been softened to intended-use/affordance statements; no medium is asserted to be superior.

The original correctAnswer listed 'makes' both as an acceptable reading of = and as the operator misconception; the rewrite uses 'is the same as' as the consistent target and does not present 'makes' as a correct reading.
Arithmetic in the balance/true-false examples was checked: 5 = 3 + 2, 4 + 1 = 3 + 2, 3 + 2 = 2 + 3 and 7 = 3 + 4 are true; 3 + 2 = 2 + 1 and 4 + 1 = 2 + 2 are false.

probeDeeper: Is 5 = 3 + 2 allowed, or does it have to be 3 + 2 = 5? Why?
Point to the part of your sentence that shows the two more ducks arriving.
What does the = sign tell us about the two sides?
Could you write a take-away story and a number sentence with a − sign?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads 'three plus two equals five'; offers 3 + 2 = 5 (or 5 = 3 + 2) for the ducks; reads = as 'is the same as' / 'makes' / 'is equal to' — not merely 'the answer is'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads = as 'the answer is' / 'makes the total' (operator view), so cannot cope with the sum on the right or a missing addend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a balance and 'is the same as' language; show true/false equations with the total first (5 = 3 + 2) so = is read relationally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child calls 5 = 3 + 2 'backwards' or wrong, and expects an answer straight after the = sign.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses or misnames + and − — reads − as 'and', or maps a symbol to the wrong action.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair each symbol with its action in context repeatedly (joining → plus, taking away → minus); do not just label symbols on flashcards.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reads 3 − 2 as 'three plus two', or acts out combining for a minus.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses or mirror-writes symbols/numerals when writing the sentence, though spoken reading is correct.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT treat as a maths misunderstanding or drill correction — reversals are a normal early-writing stage; model correct orientation and it resolves with time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Digits or symbols written back-to-front, or the sentence written right-to-left, while the child reads it correctly aloud.

responseLevels.gap: Misnames + / −, or reads = only as 'the answer is' and cannot narrate a situation with the symbols.
responseLevels.full: Uses +, − and = fluently to narrate and record situations, and treats = relationally as 'is the same as', coping with sums written either way round.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes a standard left-to-right sum correctly but is thrown by = with the total on the right or a missing number.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Read this out loud and tell me what is happening: 3 + 2 = 5. Now here is a story — three ducks are swimming and two more come to join them. Say a number sentence for the story, and tell me what the = sign means here.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Listen for how the child USES the symbols in context, not whether they can define them. A child with the relational meaning of = says 'is the same as' and is untroubled by 5 = 3 + 2; a child with the operator misconception reads = as 'the answer is' and expects the total to come immediately after it. Narrating a real situation with the symbols reveals genuine command.
