topic.name: Number bonds to 9
topic.description: Find the number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9 (number bonds to 10)
evidence: Given 7, respond '3' to make 10
Use a ten-frame to find the complement to 10
Record pairs that make 10 as equations (e.g. 6 + 4 = 10)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and needs 10 for a recipe, can they quickly tell you they need 4 more — without counting all the way up from 1?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1). Number bonds to 10: find the number that makes 10 when added to a given number 1-9 (7→3, 6→4). A high-centrality node (0.26) — bonds to 10 are the pivot for the making-ten strategy, column carrying, and mental calculation throughout KS1/KS2.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20'; non-statutory: 'memorise and reason with number bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.4 'for any number 1-9, find the number that makes 10 when added…'; 1.OA.6 fluency within 10.
• Operational details — Treat bonds to 10 as the special part-whole case where the whole is fixed at 10, using a structure (ten-frame) whose 'gaps' make the complement visible. Drive toward RECALL via the ten-frame image, not counting: a filled 7 leaves 3 empty cells — the child should eventually 'see' the 3. Record each pair as an equation and connect the addition bond to its subtraction partner (7+3=10, 10−7=3). Aim for rapid, both-directions recall.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): given a ten-frame with some filled, say how many more make 10. Tier B (age 5): given a number 1-9, name its bond to 10 with the ten-frame image. Tier C (age 5-6): recall all bonds to 10 quickly without the frame and give the related subtraction fact.
bestPractices: Use the ten-frame as the canonical structure so the complement is SEEN as empty cells, moving children from counting-on to recognising the bond.
Practise both directions and link addition to subtraction (7 + 3 = 10 ⇔ 10 − 7 = 3) so bonds are a fact family, not a one-way fact.
Work systematically through the pairs (1+9, 2+8, …) to reveal the symmetry and give a sense of the complete set.
Build toward automaticity through frequent short retrieval practice grounded in the ten-frame image, not isolated rote drill divorced from meaning.
Connect to bonds to 20 and the making-ten strategy explicitly so children see WHY these facts are worth knowing by heart.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame with filled and empty cells showing a number and its complement
Part-part-whole model with the whole fixed at 10
Rekenrek (two rows of 5) for showing bonds to 10
Bead string of 10 partitioned into two colours
Systematic equation list of all bonds to 10 (1+9 … 9+1)
commonMisconceptions: Counting on from the given number every time rather than recalling the bond, so speed never develops.
Knowing 7 + 3 = 10 but not the related 10 − 7 = 3 (bond not held as a fact family).
Confusing bonds to 10 with bonds to other totals when the ten-frame isn't present.
Thinking there is only one 'way to make 10' rather than a full set of pairs.
Miscounting the empty cells on the ten-frame, giving a complement off by one.

learn.summary: Number bonds to 10 for ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1): for any number 1-9, find the number that makes 10 when added to it (7→3, 6→4). The ten-frame is the key structure because the empty cells make the complement visible, moving children from counting-on to seeing/recalling the bond. Bonds should become a fact family linking addition and subtraction (7+3=10 ⇔ 10−7=3) and be built toward rapid both-directions recall, because they underpin the making-ten strategy, column carrying and mental calculation through KS1/KS2.

activities.title: Ten-frame 'make ten' practice
feedback: If the child recounts the counters and counts on by ones (7, 8, 9, 10) to get 3, direct attention to the group of empty cells as the answer; if it helps, show the same split on a part-part-whole model with the whole fixed at 10 so the complement is seen rather than counted.
If the child answers the total (10) or the starting number (7), physically fill the frame and name just the added part; contrast 'how many altogether' with 'how many MORE to make 10'.
When a bond is instant, name it as a known fact; when a bond is still counted, add it to short retrieval practice so all bonds become fast.
Praise reading the complement straight off the empty cells, not the counting route.
activities.rationale: The ten-frame makes complements to 10 visible and supports the shift from counting to recognition; recording the equation ties the seen structure to the symbolic bond. An interactive or physical frame allows repeated predict-then-check reps that a single fixed picture does not.
sourceClaims: The ten-frame makes complements to 10 visible and supports the shift from counting to recall; fluency should grow from meaningful structure, not rote-only drill.
Y1 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20, and memorise/reason with bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms.
learnerActions: Look at a ten-frame holding some counters (e.g. 7 counters, so 3 cells are empty).
Before counting, predict how many more counters are needed to make 10.
Add (drag, tap, or place physical counters) the missing counters to fill the frame to 10, then check.
Say and record the matching equation, e.g. 7 + 3 = 10.
Repeat with different starting numbers 1-9, working toward naming the complement without counting the empty cells one by one.
activities.intendedInsight: The empty cells of the ten-frame ARE the answer: once the ten-frame becomes a mental picture, the complement is recognised at a glance rather than counted up.

activities.title: Link each bond to its subtraction partner
feedback: If the child knows 7+3=10 but cannot give 10−7=3, physically take 7 away from a full frame and let them see the 3 that remains.
If the child treats the reversed addition as a new unknown, fill the frame with two colours (e.g. 7 red, 3 yellow) and turn it around so the 3 comes first: the same two parts still make 10.
Confirm answers against the filled/unfilled frame so the subtraction is seen, not guessed.
activities.rationale: Bonds held as fact families (both addition and the related subtraction) are more flexible and support later subtraction and mental calculation; practising both directions prevents one-way knowledge.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20, and memorise/reason with bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms.
K.OA.4: for any number 1-9 find the number that makes 10; 1.OA.6 add/subtract fluently within 10 including making ten.
learnerActions: Start from a known bond shown on a ten-frame, e.g. 7 + 3 = 10.
Remove the added part (the 3) and state the matching subtraction fact: 10 − 3 = 7.
Also state the commutative partner, 3 + 7 = 10, and the other subtraction fact, 10 − 7 = 3 (take away the 7 to see the 3 that remains).
Write the full fact family for the pair.
Answer quick questions in both directions, e.g. '__ + 6 = 10' and '10 − 6 = __'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each pair that makes 10 is one fact family, not several separate facts: knowing 7+3 means you also know 3+7, 10−7 and 10−3.

activities.title: Work through the complete set systematically
feedback: If the child thinks there is only one way to make 10, show several pairs side by side.
If the child confuses bonds to 10 with other totals, bring the frame, rekenrek or ten-bead structure back so the whole is clearly fixed at 10.
Highlight the symmetry so half the set only needs to be learned once.
activities.rationale: Seeing the organised, symmetric set gives a sense of completeness and reduces the load of memorising, and it exposes the misconception that only one pair makes 10.
learnerActions: Notice the symmetry (each pair appears both ways around) and that 5+5 is the one pair of equal parts.
Use a partitioned ten-strand, a two-colour ten of beads, or one row of a rekenrek (ten beads grouped as five and five in two colours) to show the same pairs physically.
Keep a reference display of the full set and tap/reveal a partner for any starting number.
Tell the whole set from memory as it becomes secure.
activities.intendedInsight: There is a complete, finite set of ways to make 10 with its own symmetry — not just one 'way to make 10' and not an endless list.

activities.title: Short, fast retrieval practice for automaticity
feedback: Treat a slow or counted answer as a cue to rehearse that specific bond, not as failure.
When recall is patchy (fast for 7→3 but counted for 4→6), rehearse the weaker bonds to automaticity; do not reteach the whole concept if it is already understood.
Keep the pace brisk and the stakes low so retrieval stays enjoyable.
activities.rationale: Retrieval practice builds automaticity, but it rehearses recall rather than building the underlying concept, which should already be established with the ten-frame. Recognition/matching formats check familiarity but do not require the child to construct the bond unaided, so include production items (say or write the complement).
sourceClaims: The ten-frame makes complements to 10 visible and supports the shift from counting to recall; fluency should grow from meaningful structure, not rote-only drill.
learnerActions: Answer quick-fire 'make ten' items with the frame gradually hidden, e.g. shown '7' respond '3'.
Fill in missing-number sentences such as '__ + 6 = 10' and include a related subtraction such as '10 − 2 = __'.
Match starting numbers to their partners that make 10.
Aim for quick answers from memory, returning to the ten-frame image whenever a bond is uncertain.
activities.intendedInsight: Frequent, low-stakes retrieval turns worked-out complements into instantly recalled facts.

activities.title: Talk-it-through quick-fire (oral reasoning)
feedback: If reasoning reveals counting-on, return to the frame and the empty-cell image.
Use oral questions as a quick check and warm-up, alongside written/visual practice for the many fast repetitions automaticity needs.
activities.rationale: Oral dialogue surfaces the child's method and reasoning; it is a useful complement to, not a replacement for, frequent practice.
learnerActions: Answer spoken 'how many more to make 10?' questions for various starting numbers.
Explain how the ten-frame helped: 'I saw three empty cells.'
Answer a follow-up that checks the fact family: 'If 7 and 3 make 10, what do 3 and 7 make?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to say how you found the complement shows whether the child is seeing the structure or still counting.

constraints: Aim for recall grounded in the ten-frame image, not isolated rote drill divorced from meaning.
Recognition and matching formats check familiarity but do not require independent construction; include items where the child must say or write the complement unprompted.
A fixed reference display of the full set is useful for looking up a partner but does not provide the repeated retrieval needed for recall; pair it with active practice.
Oral quick-fire alone cannot efficiently deliver the many fast repetitions automaticity requires; use it as a check and warm-up alongside visual/written practice.
Physical counters, bead strings and the rekenrek are concrete supports; the goal is to fade the structure so the child answers from the remembered image or known fact.
Before fading the frame, ensure the child can parse 'how many MORE to make 10' as distinct from 'how many altogether'.

topic.description: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way (part-part-whole)
evidence: Use objects or drawings to find all pairs that make a given number

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 8 grapes, can they split them into two groups in different ways — like 3 and 5, or 4 and 4 — and explain that both groups together still make 8?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), CONCEPTUAL. Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in MORE THAN ONE WAY (part-part-whole): 5 = 1+4 = 2+3 = 0+5… A high-centrality node (0.26) — flexible decomposition underpins number bonds, bridging-through-ten, and subtraction-as-unknown-part.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1 non-statutory): pupils 'memorise and reason with number bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms'; part-whole reasoning is foundational to bonds.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.3 'decompose numbers less than or equal to 10 into pairs in more than one way… and record with a drawing or equation (e.g. 5 = 2 + 3 and 5 = 4 + 1)'; K.OA.4 finding the missing part to make 10.
• Operational details — Fix the WHOLE, then systematically vary the split, recording each as an equation, so the child sees a number is not one fixed pair but a family of pairs. Work systematically (5 as 0+5, 1+4, 2+3…) to reveal the pattern and build confidence that all pairs have been found. Emphasise the whole staying constant while the parts trade — the conservation idea behind bonds and later regrouping.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): find at least two different pairs that make a given number with objects. Tier B (age 5): find several pairs for a number up to 10 and record them as equations. Tier C (age 5-6): work systematically to find ALL pairs for a number and explain that the whole stays the same while the parts change.
bestPractices: Keep the WHOLE fixed and physically trade objects between the two parts, so children see the same total split many ways — the conceptual heart of the topic.
Work systematically (0+5, 1+4, 2+3, …) and record each split as an equation, so the set of pairs is seen as complete and patterned, not random.
Use the part-part-whole frame consistently so 'whole' and 'part' become stable ideas that carry into missing-part subtraction and bonds.
Connect to commutativity gently (2+3 and 3+2 use the same pair) without yet formalising it, and to the emerging idea that knowing one pair gives its partner.
Record with drawings AND equations so the abstract bond is tied to a picture of two parts making a whole.
keyRepresentations: Part-part-whole ('cherry'/bar) model with a fixed whole and two changeable parts
Ten-frame showing a number split by colour into two parts
Bead string or two-colour counters partitioned into two groups
A systematic list/table of all pairs for a number (0+5, 1+4, …) with equations
Rekenrek (arithmetic rack) for showing splits of 5 and 10
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number has only ONE decomposition (e.g. 5 is 'just' 4 and 1) and not seeing it as a family of pairs.
Losing the whole — changing a part but not compensating the other, so the total drifts (5 becomes 2+4).
Missing pairs or double-counting when not working systematically, so 'all the ways' is never securely established.
Treating 2+3 and 3+2 as entirely unrelated rather than the same pair reordered.
Not connecting decomposition to subtraction — failing to see that if 5 = 2 + 3 then 5 − 2 = 3.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build flexible decomposition of numbers up to 10 into part-pairs (part-part-whole): 5 = 0+5 = 1+4 = 2+3, and their reversals. The core insight is that one whole is a FAMILY of pairs — the whole stays constant while the two parts trade. Fix the whole, systematically vary the split, and record each as an equation, connecting to number bonds and missing-part subtraction. Several complementary formats each play a role: concrete manipulatives and a screen part-whole bench both let the child generate pairs and feel the whole conserved, while a static anchor diagram and recognition checks consolidate the bond facts. Physical manipulation is emphasised at this age in line with the curriculum.

activities.title: Part-whole bench: slide the divider, keep the whole
feedback: If the child offers only one split, model several splits of the same 5 and record each as an equation; establish that all are correct and the whole is unchanged.
If a re-split uses more or fewer than 5 counters, anchor that all 5 must be used every time; count the whole before and after each split to see it is conserved.
If splits are found at random with repeats or omissions, scaffold a systematic order (0+5, 1+4, 2+3, …); this is an organisation prompt, not a concept reteach.
Ask: when you split 5 into 1 and 4, how many counters in total? And when it is 2 and 3? — to surface conservation of the whole.
Ask: is 4 and 1 a different way from 1 and 4, or the same? — to gently connect reversals to the same pair.
Ask: have we found all the ways, and how could we be sure? — to motivate systematic searching.
activities.rationale: A movable-divider model with live-updating part numbers and an equation lets the child generate decompositions and watch the two parts change while the whole stays fixed, making conservation and the pair-family idea observable. The found-pairs tally supports systematic searching, and a subtraction toggle links decomposition to missing-part subtraction. The live recolouring, dragging, running tally, and subtraction toggle are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required product features; equivalent hands-on counters and a written list achieve the same aim.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils memorise and reason with number bonds within 20 in several forms, resting on part-whole decomposition.
K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
Systematic part-whole decomposition with a conserved whole underpins number bonds and missing-part subtraction.
learnerActions: Place a fixed whole of counters (e.g. 5) into a single frame, then move a divider across so the counters fall into two parts.
Slide the divider to a new spot and read the two parts aloud (e.g. 1 and 4; then 2 and 3).
Record each split as an equation (5 = 1 + 4, 5 = 2 + 3, …) next to a drawing of the two groups.
Keep a running list of pairs found and check whether every pair has been discovered.
In a 'make 10' mode, fix the whole at 10 and find pairs that make ten.
Flip a found pair to subtraction: having built 5 = 2 + 3, state that 5 − 2 = 3.
activities.intendedInsight: A number is not one fixed pair but a whole family of pairs; the parts trade while the total is conserved, and each known pair also tells a missing-part subtraction fact.

activities.title: Physical trading with counters and a part-whole frame
feedback: If the child thinks only one decomposition is correct, model more splits of the same whole and treat each as valid.
If the total drifts, count all the counters before and after the move to show the whole is conserved.
Prompt 'can you make 5 a different way?' to push a systematic search; pair the talk with the counters so the doing stays concrete.
Note gently that 2+3 and 3+2 are the same pair reordered, without yet formalising commutativity.
activities.rationale: Hands-on trading of concrete objects — keeping the whole fixed while physically moving counters between the two parts — makes conservation tangible at this age. Representations such as ten-frames, bead strings, two-colour counters, and a rekenrek give multiple concrete views; recording with both drawings and equations ties the picture to the abstract bond. Guided talk prompts ('make 5 another way') can prompt a systematic search, but talk alone does not itself provide the physical trading, so use it alongside the manipulatives, which supply the concrete doing.
sourceClaims: Systematic part-whole decomposition with a conserved whole underpins number bonds and missing-part subtraction.
K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
learnerActions: Lay out a fixed whole of two-colour counters or a bead string and physically move one counter from one part to the other.
After each move, say the two parts and write the matching equation.
Build a systematic list of all pairs for 5, then for 10, recording each with a drawing and an equation.
Explain in your own words why the total stays the same when a counter moves across.
Show that 2+3 and 3+2 use the same two groups reordered.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically trading objects between two parts of a fixed whole makes conservation tangible: the total never changes, only how it is split.

activities.title: Anchor diagram and recognition checks
feedback: For a chosen distractor that is off by one, prompt the child to count both parts together and compare with the target whole.
For a missing-part error, return to the fixed whole and ask how many more are needed to complete it.
Treat the diagram as a ready-made display: if the child has not yet generated pairs themselves, send them back to the counters or the part-whole bench to build pairs first.
activities.rationale: A static anchor diagram offers a clean display of multiple decompositions, and recognition/fill-in tasks are useful consolidation and diagnosis of bond knowledge. These formats check and reinforce the facts; because the pairs are presented ready-made or selected rather than constructed, recognition alone does not by itself elicit independent generation, so use these tasks after generation work (a sequencing proposal, not a verified requirement) so the flexible-decomposition insight is built first.
sourceClaims: K.OA.3: decompose numbers ≤ 10 into pairs in more than one way, recording with drawings/equations (5 = 2 + 3, 5 = 4 + 1); K.OA.4 make ten.
learnerActions: Study a part-whole (cherry/bar) diagram for one number and reveal each pair in turn (tap or lift-the-flap 'another way?').
Fill in the missing part: 5 = 2 + __, and set a slider or write the number to complete the bond.

From a set of candidate pairs that also contains a distractor pair whose total is off by one (so it does not make 5), multi-select only the pairs that make 5; the distractor should be left unselected.
Match given pairs to the correct whole.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing several decompositions laid out and practising missing-part completion consolidates number-bond facts and helps spot pairs that do not make the target whole.

constraints: Primary goal is flexible, systematic generation of multiple pairs with a conserved whole; a child producing only one split or changing the total has not yet met the objective.

Recognition and fill-in tasks (multi-select, slider, matching) consolidate and diagnose bond facts but do not by themselves elicit independent generation of decompositions; use them after construction, not as a substitute for it.

A static anchor diagram presents pairs ready-made; it is a display/anchor and is proposed to follow hands-on or interactive generation so the child feels the whole conserved rather than only reading pairs off.

Guided talk prompts can support searching but do not themselves provide the physical trading or visual comparison, since the generating and comparing is still largely manual and visual at this age; pair them with a manipulative rather than relying on talk alone.

Checkpoints: Tier A (age 4) find at least two different pairs for a given number with objects; Tier B (age 5) find several pairs up to 10 and record as equations; Tier C (age 5-6) work systematically to find ALL pairs and explain the whole stays the same while parts change.

Address known misconceptions: a number having only one decomposition; losing the whole when re-splitting; missing/double-counting pairs when unsystematic; treating 2+3 and 3+2 as unrelated; and failing to connect 5 = 2 + 3 to 5 − 2 = 3.
Treat reversals (1+4 vs 4+1) as the same pair reordered; introduce commutativity only gently, not as a formal rule.
The distractor pair in recognition tasks should over- or under-shoot the target whole (e.g. off by one); never present it as a correct way to make the target.

probeDeeper: When you split 5 into 1 and 4, how many counters are there in total? And when you split it into 2 and 3?
Is 4 and 1 a different way from 1 and 4, or the same?
Have we found all the ways — how could we be sure?
If the whole were 6 instead of 5, would there be more ways or fewer?
assess.correctAnswer: Several ways — 1+4, 2+3, 0+5 (and their reversals). A child who understands part-part-whole generates more than one split and recognises that the whole (5) stays the same while the parts change.

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a number has ONE correct decomposition — offers only 2+3 and insists that is 'the' way.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model several splits of the same 5 and record each as an equation; establish that all are correct and the whole is unchanged.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child cannot produce a second split, or judges other splits as wrong.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the WHOLE when re-splitting — the second 'split' uses more or fewer than 5 counters, so the parts no longer sum to 5.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor that all 5 must be used every time; count the whole before and after each split to see it is conserved.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A later split totals 6 or 4; the child adds/removes counters mid-task.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds splits unsystematically — repeats or omits some, unsure whether all are found.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a systematic list (0+5, 1+4, 2+3 …); this is organisation, not a concept gap, so do not reteach part-part-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces two or three splits at random and cannot tell if the set is complete.

responseLevels.gap: Produces at most one split, or changes the total when re-splitting.
responseLevels.full: Generates multiple splits (ideally systematically), records them, and states that the whole is conserved while the parts vary.
responseLevels.partial: Finds two or three splits but unsystematically, or is unsure the whole stays the same across splits.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show me a way to split these 5 counters into two groups. Now show me a DIFFERENT way. How many different ways do you think you can make 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The behaviour reveals the concept: a child who thinks a number has ONE fixed split stops after one and may call others wrong; a child with part-part-whole flexibly produces several and knows the whole is conserved. Asking 'how many different ways' separates single-split thinkers from flexible decomposers.

topic.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 5
topic.description: Fluently add and subtract within 5
evidence: Answer 2 + 3 quickly without counting on fingers
Answer 5 – 2 from recall or with minimal counting
Complete a set of within-5 addition/subtraction facts accurately and quickly
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give you the answer to sums like '2 + 3' or '5 − 2' straight away, without needing to count on their fingers every time?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Reception/Y1). Fluently add and subtract within 5 — quick, accurate recall/near-recall of the small facts (2+3, 5−2). The first fluency milestone (centrality 0.18); small enough to be subitised and memorised, it seeds automaticity for all later mental calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): number bonds and related facts within 20; the small facts within 5 are the foundational subset built first.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.5 'fluently add and subtract within 5'.
• Operational details — Fluency = efficient, accurate, flexible — NOT speed alone. Build it from subitising (instantly seeing quantities to 5) and part-whole knowledge, so recall is meaningful, then use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice to firm it up. Include subtraction alongside addition and the +0 case. Avoid anxiety-inducing timed drill as the primary mechanism; interleave strategy talk with quick recall.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): subitise quantities to 5 and answer within-5 additions with minimal counting. Tier B (age 5-6): answer any within-5 addition or subtraction quickly, from recall or a fast strategy. Tier C (age 6): recall within-5 facts automatically and use them to reason (e.g. 5−2 from 2+3).
bestPractices: Build fluency FROM subitising and part-whole understanding rather than rote drill — children who can instantly see 4 as 3-and-1 recall the facts meaningfully.
Use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice (a few minutes daily) rather than long high-pressure timed tests, which can induce maths anxiety without improving learning.
Interleave addition and its inverse subtraction, and include +0/−0, so the small-fact set is complete and connected.
Represent facts on fingers, five-frames and dice/domino patterns so recall is anchored to instantly-recognisable images.
Treat fluency as accuracy + efficiency + flexibility (choosing a good strategy), not merely answering fast.
keyRepresentations: Five-frame and finger patterns for subitising quantities to 5
Dice/domino/dot patterns for instant recognition
Part-part-whole model for facts within 5
Number track 0-5 for counting-on/back where needed
Fact cards / quick-image flashes for retrieval practice
commonMisconceptions: Counting from 1 on fingers for every fact, never moving to recall — fluency stalls.
Equating fluency with speed and rushing, producing errors, or freezing under time pressure.
Knowing additions but not the related subtractions within 5.
Uncertainty with 0 (thinking 3 + 0 must change the number).
Over-reliance on one strategy (always counting on) rather than recognising known facts.

learn.summary: Help children aged 5-6 become fluent at adding and subtracting within 5 (e.g. 2+3, 5-2, 3-3, 4+0), where fluency means accurate, efficient and flexible recall built from subitising and part-whole understanding — not raw speed. The primary engine is short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval practice with quantity images (five-frames, dice/domino patterns, fingers) kept attached until recall is secure, interleaving addition with its inverse subtraction and including the +0/-0 case.

activities.title: Quick-flash fact practice from a dot pattern
feedback: If the child counts every dot (or finger) from one on each item, do NOT ban finger-counting or mark it wrong — it is a normal stage; keep exposure short and frequent, as regular subitising practice can help recall become more secure over time.
If addition is instant but subtraction is counted (2 + 3 fast, 5 − 2 slow), link the subtraction to the known addition fact as a fact family and give brief targeted subtraction practice.
If the child gives 3 for 3 − 3, or queries/refuses a zero result, act out taking all away (and adding nothing) with real objects to establish 0 as a legitimate answer.
Praise fast AND accurate recall; if the child rushes and makes errors, slow down and re-attach the pattern image rather than pushing for speed alone.
activities.rationale: Retrieval practice is the mechanism for automaticity, and anchoring facts to subitisable images (five-frames, dice, fingers) makes the recall meaningful and flexible. An adaptive flash format that speeds up on success and re-shows the image on error blends seeing with recall while keeping stakes low.
sourceClaims: Within-5 (and within-20) number facts are built for fluent recall in Y1, from number bonds and related facts.
Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: A five-frame, dice or domino pattern (e.g. four dots) appears briefly, then the child says or taps the answer to a fact tied to it (e.g. 4 + 1, or 5 − 1 from the same image).
Keep answering a short daily set of items in a few minutes, mixing addition and subtraction.
When a fact is answered quickly and correctly, show the image more briefly next time; when the child hesitates or errs, re-show the pattern longer and talk through what they see.
Include zero cases such as 4 + 0 and 3 − 3 in the mix.
activities.intendedInsight: A child can stop counting dots one by one and simply KNOW a pattern's value, then flip the same image into a subtraction (5 − 1 = 4). Recall becomes meaningful because it is anchored to an instantly-recognisable quantity image.

activities.title: Periodic low-stakes fact check
feedback: Keep stakes low and framing calm; a check that feels like a high-pressure timed test can induce anxiety without improving learning.
Use the results to target the specific lagging facts (often subtractions) with more flash practice, rather than repeating everything.
activities.rationale: A short fact check is an honest probe of automaticity and complements daily retrieval practice, but a fixed linear item set is less adaptive and can feel high-stakes, so it suits periodic use rather than as the main practice engine. Recognition-format items confirm what is recalled but do not by themselves build automaticity.
sourceClaims: Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: Work through a short set of image-supported fact items (multiple-choice or fill-the-blank) that interleave addition and subtraction within 5, including a zero case.
Treat this as an occasional check of what has become automatic, not the daily practice engine.
After answering, note which facts were known instantly and which were worked out.
activities.intendedInsight: Children and adults can see which within-5 facts are now recalled automatically and which still need practice, especially any subtraction or zero facts that lag.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up and subitising reference
feedback: If the child counts from one or hesitates, point to the matching dot/five-frame pattern rather than correcting the answer harshly.
A static pattern reference supports recognition but cannot by itself drive the repeated retrieval that fluency needs, so pair it with the flash practice.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire and strategy talk interleave recall with reasoning and surface children's strategies, while a static subitising reference anchors recall to instantly-recognisable images; both support the main retrieval practice without replacing it.
sourceClaims: Fluency is accuracy, efficiency and flexibility built from strategies and subitising; frequent low-stakes retrieval beats high-pressure timed drill, which can cause maths anxiety.
learnerActions: Run a brief spoken quick-fire: 'What's 2 and 3? … 5 take away 2? … 4 and 1? … 3 take away 3?' and have the child answer aloud fast.
Ask follow-up reasoning prompts: 'Which of those did you just know, and which did you work out?', 'If 2 + 3 = 5, what is 5 − 3?', 'What happens if I add 0 to 4?'
Keep a reference chart of subitisable patterns 0-5 (five-frames, dice/dot patterns) visible to glance at when recall is uncertain.
activities.intendedInsight: Talking through which facts were known versus worked out surfaces the move from counting to recall, and connects each subtraction to its related addition.

constraints: Fluency means accuracy + efficiency + flexibility (choosing a good strategy), not speed alone; avoid making timed drill the primary mechanism, as time pressure can induce maths anxiety without improving learning.
Do not ban or penalise finger-counting from one — it is a normal developmental stage that, for many children, gives way to recall with regular short subitising and retrieval practice.
Build recall FROM subitising and part-whole understanding, not rote drill, so facts are meaningful; keep the quantity image attached until recall is secure.
Always interleave subtraction with addition and include the +0/-0 case so the small-fact set is complete and connected.

A static dot/five-frame reference aids recognition but cannot by itself drive repeated retrieval; oral quick-fire struggles to deliver enough varied fast reps, so each works best alongside frequent short practice.
A recognition-only check (multiple-choice) confirms what is recalled but does not by itself build automaticity; use it periodically, not as the daily engine.

The original claimed an adaptive flash game grows fluency 'in a way a fixed medium cannot' and rated a static image and oral dialogue as weaker; these are catalog fit judgements, not established comparative efficacy. Treated here as a reasonable design proposal with stated affordances/limits rather than a universal law.

Of the cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the CCSS K.OA.5 and the Baroody/Boaler/NCETM claims are marked unverified in the source row and should not be read as independently confirmed. The CCSS K.OA.5 claim is not used as an activity sourceClaim because it only restates the objective/topic rather than supporting a teaching principle; the retained DfE claim is partly a curriculum statement and only indirectly supports the retrieval-practice rationale.

Self-audit of the facts used: 2+3=5, 5-2=3, 4+1=5, 3-3=0, 5-1=4, 5-3=2, 3+0=3, 4+0=4 all check out; the diagnostic/correct-answer set (5, 3, 5, 0) is consistent. The 5 − 1 = 4 fact tied to a four-dot image is coherent with the four-dot pattern shown.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT ban finger-counting or mark it wrong — recall automates with regular short exposure and subitising practice; it is a normal stage.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1). Recall number bonds — addition AND related subtraction facts — within 20: know pairs of single-digit numbers summing up to 20 and derive the subtractions (8+5=13, 13−5=8). Extends bonds-to-10 to the full within-20 set; the fact base for KS1 mental calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20'; non-statutory: memorise and reason with bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms (9+7=16; 16−7=9; 7=16−9).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20; 1.OA.8 work with the unknown in various positions.
• Operational details — Present bonds as FACT FAMILIES from the start: each bond generates two additions and two subtractions and can be written with the unknown anywhere (7=16−9). Build recall from bonds to 10 plus bridging (making-ten) and doubles, then firm up with retrieval practice. The deliberate inclusion of related subtraction is the point — subtraction facts should come from known additions, not be learned separately.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): recall bonds to 10 and derive some within-20 sums via making ten. Tier B (age 5-6): recall within-20 bonds and give the related subtraction fact. Tier C (age 6): flexibly state any member of a within-20 fact family, including missing-number forms (7 = 16 − ?).

activities.title: Fact-family machine: one relationship, four facts
feedback: If a child recalls 8+5 fluently but re-counts 13−5 from scratch, prompt 'think of the addition — 8 and 5 make 13, so 13 take away 5 leaves...' and point to the same triangle.
If a child rejects 7 = 16 − 9 because '= means the answer comes next', re-read it as 'what goes with 9 to make 16?' and show both the 9+7=16 and the 7=16−9 forms around the same whole.
If a child counts on by ones for a crossing-ten sum, model making ten (8+2+3 for 8+5) using one full and one partial ten-frame, then return to recall.
If a child confuses bonds of different totals, re-anchor each fact to its clearly labelled whole in the part-whole model before practising.
activities.rationale: A manipulable part-whole/triangle model makes the four-facts structure explicit and lets the child regenerate the whole family, which supports relational understanding of the equals sign and deriving subtraction from addition. Live rewriting and 'cover a corner' missing-number practice are concrete ways to show the structure and target the equals-sign misconception; they are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only route.

learnerActions: Set a whole of 13 with two parts, 8 and 5, in a part-whole triangle (whole at the top, parts in the lower corners).
Read the four facts that the relationship generates: 8+5=13, 5+8=13, 13−8=5, 13−5=8. Say each one aloud.

Change a part (e.g. make the parts 7 and 6 with whole 13) and watch all four equations rewrite, so you see the same structure holds for every bond (for a double such as 6+6=12, the four forms reduce to two different facts: 6+6=12 and 12−6=6).

Use a 'cover a corner' mode: hide one number and say the missing one. Then set a new, clearly labelled whole (e.g. whole 16 with parts 7 and 9) and practise missing-number forms such as 7 = 16 − ? and 16 − ? = 9.
Practise shaky family members again in short interleaved rounds until the four facts come quickly from recall or near-instant derivation.
activities.intendedInsight: One relationship among three numbers IS four facts: learning 8+5 gives you 13−5 and 13−8 for free, so subtraction is derived from addition rather than memorised as a separate list.

Praise a correct reconstruction (making-ten) as a valid strategy to keep available for slips, while moving toward quick recall.
activities.rationale: Grounding within-20 recall in bonds-to-10 plus bridging and doubles reduces memory load and gives a fallback strategy, matching the stated progression toward the fact base of KS1 mental calculation. Use a known double to help a near-double: 6+7 is 6+6+1 or 7+7−1.
State which facts you just KNEW and which you had to work out, then practise the worked-out ones more.
Repeat in short, frequent, mixed sessions rather than one long drill.
activities.intendedInsight: Teen bonds are not fresh rote facts: they can be derived from secure bonds to 10 using making-ten and doubles, and derivation becomes faster recall with spaced practice.

activities.title: Mixed-form retrieval practice across the fact family
feedback: Correct answers to 8+5 and 13−5 are 13 and 8; if a learner offers anything else, re-check with the part-whole whole of 13.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Add and subtract within 20 using STRATEGIES — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and using known facts. A high-centrality strategy hub (0.17): bridging through ten is the reasoning that later powers column carrying/borrowing.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): represent/use bonds and related facts within 20; Y2 derive and use related facts; bridging-ten strategies are core KS1 mental methods.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20 using 'making ten… decomposing a number leading to a ten… and relationship between addition and subtraction'; 2.OA.2.
• Operational details — Teach making-ten explicitly on the ten-frame/rekenrek: to add 8+6, fill the first frame to 10 by moving 2 from the 6, leaving 4, so 10+4. For subtraction across ten, decompose to reach ten first (13−4 → 13−3 to 10, then −1). Emphasise ten as a friendly landmark. This is about REASONING to a fact, bridging the gap between counting and full recall (within-20).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): use a ten-frame to make ten when adding a bridging fact (8+6). Tier B (age 6-7): explain a making-ten or decompose-to-ten step for a within-20 fact. Tier C (age 7): choose flexibly between making-ten, near-doubles and known facts, and derive subtractions from additions.
bestPractices: Teach making-ten physically on two ten-frames/a rekenrek: children MOVE counters to complete the first ten, seeing why 8+6 becomes 10+4.
For subtraction bridging ten, model decomposing to land on ten first (13−4 = 13−3−1), so ten is the landmark in both directions.
Frame ten as a 'friendly number' and connect making-ten to the bonds-to-10 facts children already know.
Encourage strategy flexibility — near-doubles, known facts and making-ten — and discuss which is efficient for a given calculation.
Use the empty number line to record bridging jumps (+2 to 10, then +4), linking strategy to a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.
keyRepresentations: Two ten-frames showing one filled to 10 and the extra spilling into the second
Rekenrek for shifting beads to make ten
Empty number line with a jump to 10 then beyond
Part-whole model decomposing the second addend (6 = 2 + 4)
Bead string of 20 partitioned at the ten
commonMisconceptions: Counting on/back in ones across ten instead of using ten as a landmark (slow and error-prone at the boundary).
Splitting the wrong addend or splitting it wrongly when making ten (e.g. taking 4 not 2 from the 6 to fill an 8).
For subtraction, decomposing incorrectly across ten (13−4 done as 13−4 in ones with a boundary error).
Not connecting making-ten to known bonds to 10, so the strategy feels arbitrary.
Applying making-ten rigidly even when a known fact or near-double would be quicker.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2): add and subtract within 20 using strategies — making ten (8+6 = 8+2+4 = 14), decomposing to bridge ten (13−4 = 13−3−1 = 9), and deriving from known facts. The core insight is treating ten as a friendly landmark reached in both directions; this bridging reasoning later underpins column carrying and borrowing. The focus is the method, not just a correct answer, since counting all by ones can reach 14 without showing the intended understanding.

activities.title: Make ten by moving counters on a double ten-frame
feedback: If the leftover is wrong (answer 12 or 16), count exactly how many counters spill past ten and rehearse partitioning the second addend: 6 = 2 + 4, so only 2 cross to the 8.
If a child takes the wrong amount (e.g. 4 from the 6 to fill an 8), ask: how many empty cells does the first frame have? Move exactly that many.
Connect the move to bonds they know: 8 needs 2 to make 10, which is the pair 8+2 they already recognise.
If a child counts on in ones across ten, model the make-ten move on two frames so ten becomes the landmark rather than a boundary counted through.
activities.rationale: Physically completing the first ten and watching the second addend split lets children perform and see the partition-and-recombine, linking the strategy to bonds-to-10 they already know. The number line records the bridging jump in a spatial model that scales to larger numbers.

1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20 using making ten, decomposing a number leading to a ten, and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
Making-ten and decompose-to-ten strategies, taught on ten-frames/rekenreks with the empty number line, build bridging reasoning that underpins later column methods.
learnerActions: Set out 8 counters in the first ten-frame (two cells empty) and 6 in the second to add 8 + 6.
Move 2 counters from the 6 across to fill the first frame to 10, and notice the 6 has broken into 2 and 4.
Read the result as 10 + 4 = 14, and say aloud which part you moved and why.
Record the same move on an empty number line as a jump of +2 to reach 10, then +4 to reach 14.
Repeat with other bridging facts (e.g. 7+5, 9+6), each time completing the first ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Making ten is a MOVE: reorganising an awkward fact around the friendly ten (8+6 becomes 10+4) shows WHY the strategy works, not just that it gives 14.

activities.title: Bridge down to ten for subtraction
feedback: A common error is subtracting to ten and then ADDING the remainder (13 − 3 = 10, then +1 → 11). Both parts must be subtracted: after reaching 10, take the remaining 1 away, not add it, so 13 − 4 = 9.
If a child answers 11, track the 4 explicitly as 3-then-1 BOTH removed, using number-line jumps backward to and past ten.
If a child subtracts in ones and makes a boundary slip, slow down at ten and say the two jumps separately.
activities.rationale: Modelling subtraction as decompose-to-ten makes ten the landmark in both directions and prevents the frequent boundary error of losing track of how much is left to subtract.

learnerActions: To work out 13 − 4, start at 13 and first subtract enough to land on 10: 13 − 3 = 10.
Then subtract the rest: the 4 was split into 3 and 1, so take the remaining 1, giving 10 − 1 = 9.
Show both jumps back on a number line — back to 10, then one more past it.
Check you have subtracted the whole amount (3 + 1 = 4), not just part of it.
Try more subtractions that cross ten (12−5, 15−7), each time stepping onto ten first.
activities.intendedInsight: Ten is a landmark in BOTH directions: decomposing the number being subtracted so you land on ten first keeps the calculation accurate across the boundary.

activities.title: Explain and compare strategies aloud
feedback: If a child applies make-ten rigidly where a known fact or near-double is quicker, acknowledge their method then ask whether another way would be faster here.
If the strategy feels arbitrary, link it back to bonds to 10 the child already knows so making ten feels purposeful.
Praise a correct method even when the arithmetic needs a nudge, and separately correct the number slip.
activities.rationale: Socratic questioning may elicit and refine a child's bridging method and probe flexibility, and relating additions to subtractions reflects the 1.OA.6 emphasis on the relationship between the two operations.

learnerActions: Talk through how you worked out 8 + 6, step by step: which number did you split, and what did that make?
Answer probing questions: 'Why did you take 2 across to the 8 — what does that make?' and 'For 13 − 4, why break the 4 into 3 and 1?'
Offer a second method for 8 + 6 (e.g. treat it as a near-double: move 1 from the 8 to the 6 to make the double 7 + 7 = 14, or use 6 + 6 + 2, or a known fact) and say which felt quicker.
Use a known addition fact to derive a subtraction: if 8 + 4 = 12, explain how that gives 12 − 8 = 4.
Describe how a ten-frame shows what is happening in your method.
activities.intendedInsight: Because this is a reasoning strategy, explaining and comparing methods builds flexibility — children learn to choose making-ten, a near-double or a known fact according to the calculation, and to see addition and subtraction as related.

activities.title: Fill the bridging step
feedback: This checks the recorded steps; it does not by itself build the reorganisation insight, so pair it with hands-on making-ten first.
If the blank is wrong, return to moving counters to see exactly how the second number splits.
activities.rationale: Fill-in-the-step items can assess whether a child can carry out and articulate the intermediate bridging step, as a complement to hands-on construction rather than a replacement for it.
learnerActions: Complete the make-ten decomposition: 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + ___ , then give the total.
Complete a subtraction decomposition: 13 − 4 = 13 − 3 − ___ , then give the answer.
Say which number got split and why that amount was chosen.
activities.intendedInsight: Recording the intermediate bridging step makes the strategy's structure explicit and checkable.

constraints: Assess the METHOD, not just the answer: a correct 14 reached by counting all by ones does not demonstrate making-ten. Watch how the child reaches the answer.
Reaching ten first requires splitting the correct number: for 8 + 6 only 2 (not 4) crosses to the 8, matching the first frame's two empty cells.
In subtraction bridging, both parts of the decomposed amount must be SUBTRACTED (13 − 3 then − 1 = 9); subtracting to ten and then adding the remainder gives the wrong answer 11.
Fill-in-the-step and recognition tasks check recorded steps but do not elicit the hands-on reorganisation; use them after children have performed the move with counters.
A static worked example of a bridging split anchors the strategy but does not let a child perform the move on varied facts; treat it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.
Counters, paper ten-frames, bead strings and number lines are all suitable concrete media; an on-screen draggable version is one option, not a requirement.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer sums like '7 + 3' or '9 − 4' almost instantly — without stopping to count on their fingers?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y1/Y2). Fluently add and subtract within 10 — quick, accurate, flexible recall of all facts to 10. A high-centrality fluency hub (0.17); automaticity here frees working memory for the making-ten strategy and all larger calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1/Y2): number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20 (facts within 10 the core subset); Y2 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 'add and subtract within 20… demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10'.
• Operational details — Extend within-5 fluency using derived-fact strategies: bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1. Push from counting toward recall via the ten-frame image and known-fact reasoning, then consolidate with short frequent retrieval practice. Include all subtraction facts and link them to their addition partners (fact families). Fluency = efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): answer within-10 additions using a fast strategy (bonds, doubles) rather than counting all. Tier B (age 6-7): recall any within-10 fact quickly and give its related subtraction. Tier C (age 7): use within-10 facts fluently to reason about larger calculations (e.g. 6+7 via 6+6+1).
bestPractices: Anchor fluency in derived-fact strategies (bonds to 10, doubles/near-doubles, +0/+1) so facts are recalled meaningfully and reconstructable if forgotten.
Use the ten-frame image and rekenrek to move children from counting to 'seeing' facts, then fade the support.
Teach addition and subtraction as fact families (6+4=10, 10−4=6) so subtraction facts come from known additions.
Consolidate with short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval rather than long timed tests; interleave facts so children discriminate rather than pattern-guess.
Model choosing an efficient strategy for each fact (flexibility), not one method for all.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame(s) for facts and complements within 10
Rekenrek (two rows of 5) for doubles and bridging
Doubles/near-doubles visual (two equal rows, one extra)
Fact-family triangle linking a bond's + and − facts
Quick-image flash cards for retrieval practice
commonMisconceptions: Persisting with count-all/count-on for every fact instead of using derived facts or recall.
Mastering additions but not the related subtractions within 10.
Treating fluency as pure speed, leading to errors under pressure or anxiety.
Not recognising doubles/near-doubles as a shortcut (computing 6+7 from scratch).
Confusing similar facts (7+2 vs 7+3) when practice isn't interleaved.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, build fluent (efficient, accurate, flexible) addition and subtraction within 10, moving children from counting toward recall and derived-fact reasoning (bonds to 10, doubles and near-doubles, +/−0 and +/−1). Anchor facts in strategies so a forgotten fact can be reconstructed, link each addition to its subtraction partner as fact families, and consolidate with short, frequent, interleaved retrieval. The primary proposal is adaptive strategy-anchored retrieval practice with fading visual support; a fixed quiz, a static strategy anchor, and oral quick-fire are preserved as complementary tools with different purposes.

activities.title: Adaptive fluency practice with fading ten-frame support
feedback: If the child counts on each item, do not drill for speed under pressure or penalise counting; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and point to the known bond or double behind the fact — with continued short, frequent practice, automaticity typically develops.
If the child counts up from the smaller addend (e.g. 2 + 7 counted 3,4,5,6,7,8,9), prompt 'start from the bigger number' — this is an efficiency habit (commutativity), not a missing fact.
If complements to ten are slow (10 − 6 counted), pause and re-secure number bonds to 10 to automaticity; the rest of within-10 may already be fine.
When a fact is answered instantly, let the supporting image fade further so the child notices they now 'just know' it.
activities.rationale: Brief, low-pressure, strategy-anchored retrieval with fading support and interleaving is a key route to building meaningful automaticity; adaptivity lets support fade as recall strengthens and surfaces strategy hints when a child stalls.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
1.OA.6: add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency within 10, using strategies such as making ten, decomposing, and relationships between + and −.
learnerActions: Answer within-10 facts presented one after another (e.g. 6 + 4, 7 + 2, 9 − 4, 10 − 6), aiming to say the answer without counting.
Start with a faint ten-frame (or rekenrek image) behind each fact; as the child answers quickly, let the visual fade so they move from 'seeing' to recalling.
When a child stalls on a harder fact like 4 + 5, surface a strategy hint that shows the near-double (4 + 4 and one more) so they reconstruct rather than freeze.
Use a fact-family mode that surfaces the related subtraction for each bond (6 + 4 = 10 alongside 10 − 4 = 6, 10 − 6 = 4).
Interleave fact types (doubles, bonds, near-doubles, +/−1) so the child discriminates between similar facts (7 + 2 vs 7 + 3) rather than pattern-guesses.
activities.intendedInsight: A hard fact becomes easy when the child sees the double or bond inside it; isolated answers become a connected, flexible web of facts, including the subtraction partners — real fluency, not brittle speed.

activities.title: Interleaved fact quiz as a periodic check
feedback: Use results to spot which specific facts are still being counted and revisit the strategy behind them.
Favour short frequent sets over long timed tests, which can trigger errors or anxiety; fluency means efficient, accurate and flexible, not speed alone.
activities.rationale: Speeded retrieval practice drives automaticity, so fact quizzes are a legitimate practice and assessment tool; a fixed quiz is less adaptive than guided practice and is best used as a periodic check rather than the main teaching driver.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Work short sets of within-10 fact items (multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank), kept low-stakes and quick.
Include related-subtraction pairs alongside additions (e.g. 6 + 4 and 10 − 6) so both are practised.
Interleave fact types within a set rather than grouping all doubles or all bonds together.
activities.intendedInsight: Quick retrieval across mixed facts shows which facts are recalled versus still counted, and keeps subtraction facts practised alongside their addition partners.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up
feedback: Watch for recall versus counting on; the 10 − 6 item checks whether ten-facts are automatic (or whether the child counts back or counts up from 6), and the 7 + 2 item shows whether the child counts on from the larger addend.
Treat an exposed gap (e.g. ten-bonds not automatic) as the next thing to re-secure, not a reason to drill under time pressure.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire builds recall and makes reasoning audible; on its own it cannot deliver the volume of varied, adaptive repetition that written/adaptive practice provides, so it works best as a short warm-up.
learnerActions: Run a brief spoken quick-fire round of within-10 facts as a warm-up, e.g. '6 + 3? … 9 − 4? … 7 + 2? … 10 − 6?'

After an answer, ask follow-up questions: 'For 2 + 7, could you start from the 7 instead? Is it quicker?', 'How does knowing 6 + 4 = 10 help with 10 − 6?', 'Which did you just know without working out?', 'What's 9 − 4 — and how did you get it?'
activities.intendedInsight: Speaking facts aloud and explaining the strategy makes the child's recall-versus-counting visible and reinforces commutativity and fact-family links.

activities.title: Strategy reference anchor for derived facts
feedback: Use the anchor to prompt reconstruction, then return to retrieval so the child practises recalling without it.
Recognising a strategy on a wall is a scaffold; it does not by itself build the repeated retrieval that automaticity needs.
activities.rationale: A static strategy anchor aids recognition and reconstruction of facts but cannot drive repeated retrieval, so it supports rather than replaces active practice.
sourceClaims: Fluency within 10 should be built from derived-fact strategies (doubles, bonds, near-doubles) and consolidated with frequent low-stakes retrieval and interleaving.
learnerActions: Keep a visible reference wall or card of key derived facts and strategies: doubles (two equal rows), near-doubles (one extra), bonds to 10 on a ten-frame, and fact-family triangles linking a bond's + and − facts.
Point to the matching strategy when a fact is forgotten so the child reconstructs it (e.g. find 4 + 5 via 4 + 4 and one more).
activities.intendedInsight: Having the underlying strategies visible helps children recognise and reconstruct facts meaningfully instead of guessing.

constraints: Fluency means efficient + accurate + flexible, not speed alone; avoid long timed tests that cause errors or anxiety and use short, frequent, low-stakes retrieval instead.
Do not penalise counting under time pressure; model count-on-from-the-larger-number and derived-fact reasoning so automaticity develops naturally.
Include all subtraction facts within 10 and link them to their addition partners (fact families); mastering additions alone is incomplete.
Interleave fact types so children discriminate between similar facts rather than pattern-guess.
A static strategy anchor and an oral quick-fire are recognition/warm-up scaffolds; they do not by themselves deliver the repeated varied retrieval needed for automaticity.
Visual supports (ten-frame, rekenrek) should be faded as recall strengthens, not relied on permanently.
Number bonds to 10 are a prerequisite thread; if complements to ten are not automatic, re-secure number bonds to 10 rather than drilling all facts.

topic.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers
evidence: Answer any single-digit addition fact within 3 seconds

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} instantly recall all the single-digit addition facts — like '7 + 8 = 15' — without needing to count or think for more than a second?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8 (Y2/Y3). Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; KNOW FROM MEMORY all sums of two one-digit numbers. The automaticity endpoint of KS1 additive facts (centrality 0.15) — secure recall here is the platform for all multi-digit mental and written calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 'fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; by end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers'.
• Operational details — The goal is genuine automaticity: instant, accurate recall of single-digit sums and their subtraction partners, with a strategy to fall back on if a fact slips. Reach it by consolidating the within-20 strategies (making ten, doubles/near-doubles, bonds) into recalled facts through distributed, interleaved retrieval practice. Include all subtraction facts as members of fact families. Keep practice low-stakes to protect against anxiety while still valuing efficiency.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): recall most single-digit sums quickly, reconstructing the few uncertain ones via strategy. Tier B (age 7-8): recall all sums of two one-digit numbers from memory and the related subtractions. Tier C (age 8): apply recalled facts instantly to derive related facts to 100 (e.g. 8+5 → 80+50, 18+5).
bestPractices: Consolidate strategy-based within-20 work into recalled facts — automaticity should be the fluent endpoint of understanding, not rote learning bypassing it.
Use distributed, interleaved, low-stakes retrieval practice (little and often, mixed facts) which cognitive science shows builds durable recall better than massed drill.
Keep a reconstructable strategy available for slips (near-double, make-ten) so a momentarily forgotten fact isn't a dead end.
Practise subtraction facts as fact families with their additions, and stretch to derived facts to 100 to show the payoff of knowing them.
Avoid high-pressure timed testing as the main vehicle; monitor which specific facts remain non-automatic and target those.
keyRepresentations: Addition fact grid (sums of two one-digit numbers) for tracking coverage
Fact-family triangles linking each sum to its two subtractions
Doubles/near-doubles and make-ten visuals as fallback strategies
Quick-image/flash retrieval cards, interleaved
Derived-fact chains (8+5=13 → 18+5, 80+50) showing the payoff
commonMisconceptions: Still counting on/back for facts that should be recalled, indicating incomplete automaticity.
Knowing sums but not the related subtractions (fact family incomplete).
Speed-without-accuracy under timed pressure, or anxiety suppressing recall.
Treating memorised facts as disconnected from strategies, so a forgotten fact can't be reconstructed.
Failing to use known facts to derive related facts to 100 (recomputing 18+5 from scratch).

learn.summary: Ages 7-8 (Y2/Y3): build genuine automaticity with single-digit sums and their related subtractions within 20, with a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) as a fallback for slips. Practice should be distributed, interleaved and low-stakes, treat subtraction as members of fact families, and stretch to deriving related facts to 100. A workable progression is: recall most sums while reconstructing a few by strategy; then recall all sums and the related subtractions (aiming for recall within about 3 seconds); then apply recalled facts instantly to derive facts to 100. The original row recommended an adaptive fluency game; strong alternatives (speeded retrieval practice, oral quick-fire, and a static fact-grid/strategy reference) are preserved here with their distinct purposes and limits.

activities.title: Personal fact grid: track recall vs counting, little and often
feedback: If the child counts on by ones for 8+7 (9…10…11…12…13…14…15), rehearse make-ten as a bridge: 8+2=10, then 5 more is 15.
If a fact is reconstructed correctly but slowly, acknowledge it is right and re-serve it later to move it toward instant (around-3-second) recall.
If within-10 facts are secure but crossing-ten facts (8+7, 6+9) are shaky, focus practice on the crossing-ten set, mixing in only an occasional secure within-10 fact rather than re-drilling them.
Keep it low-stakes: value accuracy and strategy, not only speed, to protect against anxiety suppressing recall.
activities.rationale: Distributed, interleaved, low-stakes retrieval practice supports durable recall better than massed drill, and consolidating strategies into recalled facts keeps a fallback available. A live heatmap of mastered vs shaky facts (cells glowing green when recalled, amber when counted) and a one-tap strategy hint on hesitation are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; the same can be done on paper.
sourceClaims: Automaticity is best reached as the endpoint of strategy understanding, via distributed interleaved retrieval, with a reconstructable strategy fallback.
learnerActions: Keep a grid of single-digit sums where each cell is a fact the child is practising (e.g. the row/column for crossing-ten sums like 8+7, 6+9).
Mark a fact as secure once it is recalled instantly (roughly within 3 seconds, no counting), and as 'still counting' when the child has to count on or pause.
Return frequently and briefly to the 'still counting' facts, mixed in with secure ones, rather than drilling one fact many times in a row.

When a fact slips, rebuild it aloud with a strategy — near-double (6+9 → 'double 6 is 12, plus 3 more is 15') or make-ten (8+7 → '8+2 is 10, then 5 more is 15') — then try it again cold a little later.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity is the fluent endpoint of understanding: instant recall for most facts, with a strategy to reconstruct any that momentarily slip, so recall stays connected to reasoning rather than brittle.

activities.title: Fact families: pull each subtraction from its addition
feedback: If additions are fluent but subtractions are slow or counted, make the fact family explicit and prompt 'think of the addition' for each subtraction.
If the child re-counts 15-8 from scratch rather than linking it to 8+7=15, point back to the triangle and the known addition.
activities.rationale: A common gap is knowing sums but not the related subtractions. Practising them together as fact families closes this. Fact-family triangles make the link between one sum and its two subtractions visible. The cited standards establish that subtraction facts within 20 should be recalled fluently, but the fact-family method itself is a research-informed scaffold not asserted by the sources, so no source claim is attached here.
learnerActions: For each secure sum, state the whole fact family: from 8+7=15, give 7+8=15, 15-8=7 and 15-7=8.
Practise subtraction prompts by first thinking of the matching addition: for 15-8, think 'what plus 8 makes 15?'
Use a fact-family triangle (15 at top, 8 and 7 below) to see all four facts come from the same three numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing a sum should give the related subtractions for free; subtraction within 20 does not need recounting from scratch.

activities.title: Derive to 100: show why knowing these by heart pays off
feedback: If the child recomputes 18+5 from scratch, prompt them to reuse 8+5=13 and add the ten back (18+5 = 13+10 = 23).
If the place-value jump to 30+50 is unclear, re-express it as 'how many tens' (3 tens and 5 tens make 8 tens) before converting to 80.
activities.rationale: Deriving related facts to 100 demonstrates the usefulness of automatic recall and meets the Y2 'derive and use related facts up to 100' standard. A derived-fact bonus round can motivate this.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100.
learnerActions: Start from a recalled fact and derive related ones within 100: 8+5=13 → 18+5=23 and 38+5=43; 3+5=8 → 30+50=80.
Explain the link out loud: '3 ones plus 5 ones is 8, so 3 tens plus 5 tens is 8 tens, which is 80.'
Try a short chain of derivations from one known fact to feel the payoff of instant recall.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of single-digit facts is the platform for fast mental calculation with larger numbers (the Tier C aim of applying recalled facts to derive facts to 100).

activities.title: Speeded retrieval practice (strong alternative): short, frequent, interleaved
feedback: Report which facts remain non-automatic and feed those back into the fact-grid practice.
Avoid making high-pressure timed testing the main vehicle; use it to diagnose, not to pressure.
activities.rationale: Speeded, interleaved retrieval is a genuinely appropriate practice/assessment vehicle for 'know from memory', though a fixed set of items is less adaptive and diagnostic than interleaved practice that targets each child's shaky facts, and should stay low-stakes to avoid anxiety.
sourceClaims: Automaticity is best reached as the endpoint of strategy understanding, via distributed interleaved retrieval, with a reconstructable strategy fallback.
learnerActions: Work through short, mixed sets of single-digit sums and differences, aiming for near-instant answers (roughly within 3 seconds per fact).
Note which specific facts were not automatic so they can be targeted next time.
Keep sessions brief and frequent rather than one long high-pressure test.
activities.intendedInsight: Speeded retrieval is close to the target behaviour of 'knowing from memory' and is a useful practice and monitoring tool when kept low-stakes.

activities.title: Oral quick-fire warm-up (alternative): fast spoken recall
feedback: Use probe questions to surface method: 'How did you work out 8+7 — did you make a ten?', 'You said 8+7=15; so what is 15-8?', 'Is 6+9 easier if you think of it as 9+6? Why?'
Notice which were recalled versus built, and follow up on the built ones later.
activities.rationale: Oral quick-fire builds recall and reveals reasoning, though on its own it can't deliver as many adaptive, spaced reps or track fact-level mastery as systematic written practice.
learnerActions: Run a short quick-fire round of spoken sums and differences as a warm-up.
Mix additions with their related subtractions so fact families surface in conversation.
Ask the occasional follow-up: 'did you just know that, or did you build it?'
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken rapid recall builds fluency and lets a teacher hear strategy use directly.

activities.title: Static fact grid and strategy reference (scaffold)
feedback: If the child relies on the grid to look up answers rather than recall them, move the grid out of sight for retrieval attempts and bring it back only for reconstruction.
activities.rationale: A static reference supports strategy fallback but cannot itself generate the retrieval practice that automaticity requires; it is a support used alongside active recall.
learnerActions: Keep a fact grid and a make-ten / near-doubles strategy card visible as a reference during practice.
Glance at it only to rebuild a slipped fact, not as the primary source of answers.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference anchor supports reconstruction but is a scaffold, not a driver of recall.

constraints: Automaticity should be the fluent endpoint of strategy understanding, not rote memorisation that bypasses reasoning; keep a reconstructable strategy (make-ten, near-doubles) available for slips.
Keep practice low-stakes; avoid high-pressure timed testing as the main vehicle, which can suppress recall through anxiety.
Include all subtraction facts as members of fact families, not just additions.
A static fact grid or strategy card is a reference scaffold and does not by itself drive the retrieval practice needed for recall.

A speeded quiz is close to the target behaviour but is less adaptive and diagnostic than interleaved practice that targets each child's shaky facts; use it to monitor which specific facts are non-automatic and target those.

Optional interface features (live green/amber heatmap, one-tap strategy hints, subtraction rounds, derive-to-100 bonus) make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same practice works on paper or orally.

Focus practice on the facts that are still shaky (often crossing-ten sums); secure within-10 facts do not need repeated drilling, though they can be mixed in occasionally to keep practice interleaved and maintain them.
Treat the ~3-second recall benchmark as a guide to automaticity, not a pressure threshold to be enforced under anxiety.
