topic.description: Add three one-digit numbers using strategies including looking for pairs that make 10
evidence: Calculate 5 + 7 + 3 by first adding 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15
Add any three single-digit numbers correctly
Identify useful pairs within three addends to make the calculation easier
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 4 + 6 + 8, can they spot that 4 and 6 make 10 first, then add 8 to get 18 — rather than just adding in order from left to right?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add three one-digit numbers, using strategies including looking for a pair that makes 10 (e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15). Ages 6–7, procedural application of associativity/commutativity plus bonds to 10.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including... three one-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 fluency and 1.OA.3 strategy use; 'add three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20' with make-ten grouping as the exemplar strategy.
• Operational details: the point is strategic grouping — scan the three addends for a bond to 10 (or a double), add that pair first, then add the third. Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10 and the freedom (commutative/associative) to reorder. Teach scanning explicitly rather than defaulting to left-to-right.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds three one-digit numbers correctly by any method. Tier B (age 7) — for 5 + 7 + 3 chooses 7 + 3 first because it makes ten. Tier C (age 7+) — reliably scans any three addends for the most useful pair (ten or double) and explains the choice.
bestPractices: Teach an explicit 'scan for a pair that makes ten (or a double)' habit before adding.
Rehearse bonds to 10 to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted instantly.
Use rearrangeable counters/tiles so children physically move the useful pair together.
Contrast a make-ten route with a left-to-right route on the same triple to show the efficiency gain.
Keep sums within 20 initially so the third addition crosses ten at most once.
keyRepresentations: Three movable number tiles that can be reordered
Ten-frame that fills to ten from the chosen pair, then takes the third
Empty number line with a jump to ten then on
Bar/part-whole with three parts
Bonds-to-10 pairs chart as a scanning aid
commonMisconceptions: Always adding left-to-right and never scanning for a make-ten pair.
Not recognising a pair that makes ten because bonds to 10 aren't fluent.
Losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten.
Thinking the numbers must be added in the written order.
Miscounting when crossing ten while adding the third number by ones.

learn.summary: Teaches ages 6–7 to add three one-digit numbers efficiently by scanning for a pair that makes ten (or a double), adding that pair first, then adding on the third number — e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15. The objective is the strategic habit of scanning and reordering (supported by commutativity/associativity and fluent bonds to 10), not merely getting a correct total. Includes a hands-on manipulative core, fluency/strategy-choice practice, a narration conversation, and a worked anchor, with each scaffold's role made explicit. Interactive and efficacy details are proposed, not validated.

activities.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
feedback: When a chosen pair makes exactly ten, the two tiles fuse into a '10' and the frame fills (e.g. with a glow/click) — immediate confirmation that these two tiles make exactly ten, the pair the make-ten strategy looks for.

When the triple contains a make-ten pair but the chosen pair does not make ten (it goes past ten, e.g. 5 + 7 = 12, or falls short), the frame does not land cleanly on ten, showing why that pairing is less tidy here. The total can still be found, just by a longer route. For triples built around a double (e.g. 6 + 6 + 3, which has no make-ten pair), the double is the useful pair even though it does not fill the frame to exactly ten, so do not mark it as less tidy.
A live-updating running total tile lets the child check the sum as each tile is added.
If the third addend is lost or double-counted, prompt: set the third tile aside and bring it in last, then recount.
activities.rationale: The target is a strategic move — scan, pair, regroup — so physically reordering tiles and seeing a pair snap to ten is intended to train the scanning habit and to make the regrouping concrete through handling. Live recolouring/overflow feedback is intended to show whether a chosen pair makes ten. These interactive details are illustrative of the mechanism, proposed and not validated or required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add three one-digit numbers using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice
feedback: Confirm the efficient pair (e.g. 7 + 3) and point out that it is not the first two numbers written.
If the child selects the first two numbers by default, ask 'can you see two that make ten?' and rehearse the relevant bond.
Keep any timing light and supportive so it builds automaticity rather than anxiety.
activities.rationale: Practice with strategy-choice and quick retrieval is intended to build the automaticity that makes scanning easier. Recognition/selection items check whether the child chooses the efficient pair; they complement, but do not by themselves elicit, the hands-on reordering where the child freely moves the tiles and feels the ten form.
sourceClaims: Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.

activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose
feedback: If the child narrates adding the first two written numbers every time, highlight the ten pair and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is what's missing.
If the child insists numbers must be added in written order, demonstrate that reordering keeps the total the same (any two may be added first).
When a pair makes ten but the third number is lost or doubled, bring the third number in last and recount.
activities.rationale: Narration can reveal the underlying strategy and prompt reflection on order and choice, though a conversation alone does not have the child physically handle and reorder the addends. Best used alongside doing and watching the procedure rather than as a substitute for hands-on practice.
learnerActions: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.

activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
feedback: Point to the highlighted pair and the resulting 'ten and a bit' to anchor the method.
Note that this is an example to study: it shows the method but does not give feedback on the child's own attempts, so follow it with hands-on practice.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated and gives no feedback on the learner's own pairings, but it can provide a useful reference model of the two-step strategy. Treat it as a scaffold that precedes, not replaces, active practice.
learnerActions: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.

constraints: Keep sums within 20 initially so adding the third number crosses ten at most once.
Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10; rehearse these to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted readily.
Offer triples where the make-ten pair is NOT the first two numbers written, so the task genuinely requires scanning and reordering.
Include some triples that reward a double rather than a ten, so the habit generalises to 'useful pair', not only 'exactly ten'.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which pair is easiest) check strategy choice but do not by themselves elicit the child freely reordering and feeling the ten form; pair them with hands-on or spoken production.
The worked example is a reference anchor only: it provides no feedback on the child's attempts.
Watch for losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten; bring it in last and recount rather than reteaching the whole strategy.
A correct total alone is not evidence of the strategy — ask which two were added first to distinguish scanning from left-to-right adding.
A less useful pairing (e.g. 5 + 7 first) still reaches the correct total; frame it as slower/less tidy, not as wrong.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 5+7+3=15, 8+2+6=16, 4+9+1=14 (matches the source answer key); make-ten pairs are 7+3, 8+2, 9+1 respectively — all consistent.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing' to adding three small numbers was removed as an unsupported categorical universal; the kept point is only that this task is planar/non-spatial, so a 3D model offers no particular affordance here.
One source (CCSS-M 1.OA.3/2.OA.2) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.
The source describes timed/speeded retrieval; kept but framed as light and supportive to avoid implying speed pressure is required.
Pedagogy listed further representations (empty number line, bar/part-whole, bonds-to-10 chart) not developed into activities here; they remain legitimate scaffolds if elaborated.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for a make-ten pair (5 + 7 = 12, then + 3).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'can you see two that make ten?'; highlight bonds to 10 and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Narrates adding the first two written numbers every time; ignores the ten pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — refuses to reorder to pair the ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remind that any two may be added first (associative/commutative); demonstrate reordering keeps the total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists adding 7 + 3 first because 5 comes first on the page.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes ten with a pair but then loses or double-counts the third addend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count. Don't reteach the strategy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches ten then forgets to add the leftover number, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably total three one-digit numbers, or loses an addend when combining.
responseLevels.full: Scans the three addends, pairs the one that makes ten (or a double) first, adds the third on, and totals accurately and efficiently — explaining the choice.
responseLevels.partial: Totals correctly but always left-to-right, not spotting or using the make-ten pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, and each time tell me which two numbers you added first: 5 + 7 + 3; 8 + 2 + 6; 4 + 9 + 1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each triple contains an obvious make-ten pair that is NOT the first two numbers written. A child using the target strategy reorders to pair the ten; a child adding left-to-right can still get the totals but reveals no scanning, and is slower and more error-prone. Asking 'which two first?' exposes the strategy directly, so it discriminates even when totals are correct.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
topic.description: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction
evidence: Add 8 + 3 by starting at 8 and counting on 3 (9, 10, 11)
Subtract 12 − 3 by counting back 3 from 12 (11, 10, 9)
Explain that counting on is a way to add
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 5', can they start from 8 and count up five more — rather than starting from 1 every time?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction (8 + 3 by counting on 9,10,11; 12 − 3 by counting back 11,10,9). Ages 6–7, the bridge from counting-all to more efficient calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y1 'add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero' and count on/back; underpins Y2 mental strategies.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.5 'Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g. by counting on 2 to add 2)'; a stepping stone toward 1.OA.6 strategies.
• Operational details: teach counting ON from the larger number (start at 8, not 1) as more efficient than counting-all, and counting BACK for subtraction, tracking the number of steps. Best supported on a number line/track so the steps are visible and the child doesn't count the start as a step. This is a transitional strategy — valued, then increasingly replaced by known facts and derived facts.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds 8 + 3 by counting on from 8. Tier B (age 7) — counts back accurately for 12 − 3 and starts count-on from the larger addend for 2 + 9. Tier C (age 7+) — explains counting on as adding and chooses count-on vs count-back sensibly.
bestPractices: Teach counting ON from the larger addend, not counting all from one, as the efficiency step.
Use a number line or number track so jumps are visible and the start number isn't miscounted as a step.
Track the number of steps with fingers or marks to prevent off-by-one errors.
Model counting back for subtraction and connect it to 'one less each time'.
Treat counting on/back as a transitional strategy — celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts for efficiency.
keyRepresentations: Number line / number track with hops
Fingers used to keep track of the count of steps
Hundred square for later extension
Bead string showing jumps
'Start big, count on' prompt card
commonMisconceptions: Counting all from one instead of counting on from a number (a normal earlier stage).
Counting the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → 8,9,10 = 10), an off-by-one error.
Counting on from the first-written number rather than the larger one, making more steps than needed.
Counting in the wrong direction for subtraction.
Over-relying on counting for facts that should become instant recall.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, teach counting on for addition and counting back for subtraction as the efficiency step beyond counting-all. The core skills: start from the larger number (e.g. begin at 8 for 8+3), say the NEXT number as the first count ('9'), and track the number of steps so the start isn't miscounted. Best anchored on a visible number line/track where hops are seen and counted, then gradually replaced by known and derived facts. Target sums: 8+3=11 (count on), 12−3=9 (count back), 2+9 (start from the larger addend, 9).

activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back
feedback: If a child counts the start number as the first step (8+3 → '8,9,10' = 10), point out that 8 is where you START, and the first hop lands on 9 — count the landings, not the starting spot.
If a child starts at 1 and counts everything, gently cover the first group, say '8', and count on from there; this earlier stage matures with number sense, so model rather than drill.
For subtraction going the wrong way, link counting back to 'one less each time' and track the backward hops with fingers.
If a child always starts from the first-written number (2 for 2+9), ask which number gives fewer hops and why starting at 9 is quicker.
activities.rationale: Counting on/back is literally movement along a number line, so a track where hops are visible and counted is intended to make the strategy and the off-by-one error observable, so the child can self-correct. A live track that counts each landing (and does not count the start as a step) is intended to target the classic '8,9,10'=10 slip. Starting-number highlighting, count-on/count-back modes, and a 'start from the bigger number' prompt for commutative pairs are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete. Efficacy of this interaction is a proposal, not a tested result.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers to 20 including zero, using counting strategies.
1.OA.5 relates counting to addition and subtraction, e.g. counting on 2 to add 2.
Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.

activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start
feedback: Watch for an off-by-one answer (10 for 8+3): the result is 11 — recount the landings, not the start.
If the chosen start for 2+9 is 2, note that starting at 9 means only two hops instead of nine.
For 6+2, start at 6 and count on '7, 8' — two hops lands on 8.
activities.rationale: Fixed items give good spaced consolidation but cannot correct the count as it happens, so they work best after the live hopping activity rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.

activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
feedback: If the explanation defends counting all from one, model covering the first group and counting on, and ask which took fewer counts.
Praise explanations that connect counting on to adding and counting back to 'one less each time'.
activities.rationale: Spoken reasoning reveals the underlying strategy and lets a tutor probe the counting-all habit; it complements, rather than replaces, watched practice where the procedure is performed and tracked.
sourceClaims: Children progress from counting-all to counting-on; counting the start number as a step is a common off-by-one error, and counting-on from the larger addend is the efficiency goal.
learnerActions: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.

constraints: Counting on/back is a transitional strategy: celebrate it, then nudge toward known and derived facts so it isn't over-relied on for instant-recall facts.

Counting-all from one is a normal earlier developmental stage; model counting on but do not drill it as an error — children typically move beyond it as number sense grows with experience and modelling.
A static worked number line can anchor what counting on looks like but gives no practice tracking one's own steps, where the errors occur; use it as an anchor, not the main practice.
Recognition/multiple-choice items can check the choice of start number but do not elicit the child independently performing and tracking the count; pair them with doing and narrating.
Watching HOW the child counts is central: the overt count reveals strategy and off-by-one errors that the final answer alone can hide.

Source row flagged the US CCSS 1.OA.5 claim and the Cognitively Guided Instruction claim as verified:false; treat their cited support as unconfirmed even though they are topically relevant.

The original rated a 3D treatment 'poor' asserting '3D adds nothing'; this universal claim is not established by the row and has been dropped. A number line is naturally one-dimensional, which is a sufficient rationale without claiming 3D is universally useless.
Arithmetic checked: 8+3=11, 12−3=9, 2+9=11, 6+2=8; the off-by-one distractor (10 for 8+3) is correctly flagged as an error, not a valid answer.

probeDeeper: Why did you start counting at 8 and not at 1?
Show me on the number line how you got 12 − 3.
Which is quicker for 8 + 3 — counting everything, or counting on? Why?
For 2 + 9, which number would you start from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 11; 9; 8. Watch for the child counting ON from the larger number (starting at 8, saying '9, 10, 11'), counting BACK for the subtraction, and NOT counting the start number as a step.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts all from one rather than counting on from a number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or correct as an error — this stage self-resolves with number sense; gently model covering the first set, saying '8', and counting on, and let it mature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 8 + 3, starts at 1 and counts out all eight then all three.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the starting number as the first step (8 + 3 → '8, 9, 10' = 10).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Start the count on the NEXT number; use a number line and fingers so the start isn't a step. Not a concept reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 10; observed saying the start number as step one.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts back unreliably or in the wrong direction for subtraction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model back-counting on a number line and link to 'one less each time'; track steps with fingers.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 12 − 3 counts up, or miscounts the backward steps.

responseLevels.gap: Counts all from one, or cannot track the count reliably; frequent errors.
responseLevels.full: Counts on from the larger addend and counts back accurately, tracking the number of steps, and explains counting on as a way of adding.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on/back but with off-by-one slips, or always starts from the first-written number rather than the larger.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out and show me how you count each one: 8 + 3; 12 − 3; 6 + 2.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching HOW the child counts is the whole test: a counting-all child starts at 1 and counts every item; a counting-on child starts at 8. An off-by-one child audibly counts the start number as step one and lands on 10. The overt count reveals the strategy and the classic error in a way the answer alone cannot.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Addition in any order
topic.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order
evidence: Explain that 3 + 8 gives the same answer as 8 + 3
Use commutativity to choose the larger number to count on from
Demonstrate that subtraction is not commutative (5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 6 + 4 gives the same answer as 4 + 6, so they can always choose whichever order makes the adding easier?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), CONCEPTUAL. Understand and APPLY the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order (3+8 = 8+3), and recognise that subtraction is NOT commutative (5−3 ≠ 3−5). A central property node (0.16) — it halves the facts to learn and licenses 'put the bigger number first' to count on.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'show that addition of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of 1 number from another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract… (Commutative property of addition)'.
• Operational details — Show commutativity structurally, not as a rule to memorise: the SAME set of objects seen two ways (a rod of 3 and a rod of 8 make the same length however ordered; a part-whole with parts swapped gives the same whole). Then exploit it strategically — to add 3+8, start from 8 and count on 3. Deliberately CONTRAST subtraction (take 3 from 5 vs 5 from 3) to show order matters there, preventing over-generalisation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): show 3+8 and 8+3 give the same total with objects. Tier B (age 6-7): use commutativity to count on from the larger addend. Tier C (age 7): explain why addition is commutative but subtraction is not, with an example.
bestPractices: Demonstrate commutativity with a model that is literally unchanged by reordering — the same two rods/bars, the same part-whole with parts swapped — so it's seen as structural, not a memorised rule.
Immediately put it to work: 'start with the bigger number and count on', showing the property makes calculation easier.
Explicitly contrast subtraction (5−3 vs 3−5) so children learn the property is specific to addition and don't over-generalise 'you can swap them'.
Use it to reduce fact load — knowing 3+8 gives 8+3 — linking to fluency work.
Have children justify with a drawing or rearrangement rather than just asserting the rule.
keyRepresentations: Two number rods/bars combined, then physically swapped (same total length)
Part-part-whole model with the two parts swapped
A rotated array/ten-frame showing the same quantity two ways
Empty number line: 8 then +3 vs 3 then +8 landing on the same point
Contrast pair for subtraction (5−3 and 3−5) showing different results
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising to subtraction (thinking 5−3 = 3−5) — the key error this topic must pre-empt.
Treating a+b and b+a as different facts to learn separately.
Believing the answer changes with order because the counting process feels different.
Applying 'swap them' to word problems where order encodes meaning (start/change).
Not using commutativity strategically (counting on from the smaller number, doing more work).

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, teach the commutative property of addition structurally: the same two amounts combine to the same whole whichever order they are taken (3+8 = 8+3), then exploit this to count on from the larger addend. Deliberately contrast subtraction (5−3 ≠ 3−5) so children do not over-generalise 'you can swap them'. The core insight is invariance (the addition total holds under reordering) versus change (the subtraction result shifts), and children should justify why, not just recite a rule.

activities.title: Swap bench: watch the addition total hold
feedback: If the child expects the total to change after swapping: rebuild both orders on the SAME set of objects so there is visibly one unchanging quantity combined two ways.
If the child says 5−3 and 3−5 are the same: show that 3 cannot have 5 removed (you run out), while 5−3 = 2 can be done — so order is load-bearing for take-away.
Reinforce by asking them to predict the swapped total before revealing it, then confirm it matches.
activities.rationale: A model that is literally unchanged by reordering (same rods, same part-whole) lets children see commutativity as structural rather than a memorised rule, and contrasting subtraction in the same model targets the main over-generalisation error.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction cannot.
Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Combine two bars or rods — one of 3 and one of 8 — into a single total bar, and note the total (11).
Swap the two parts so 8 comes first and 3 second, and check whether the total bar's length changes.
On a number line, trace 8 then count on 3, and separately 3 then count on 8, and mark where each lands.
Say aloud what stayed the same and what moved: the parts traded places but the whole did not change.
Switch to subtraction: build 5 then remove 3, then try 3 then remove 5, and describe what happens when you try to take 5 from 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering the two addends rearranges the parts but leaves the whole unchanged, so a+b = b+a; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with and the result changes.

activities.title: Count on from the bigger number
feedback: If the child recounts from scratch instead of reusing the known fact: build both orders on the same counters to show it is one unchanging total, then practise stating the swapped fact immediately.
If the child counts on from the smaller number: compare how many steps each order takes to make the efficiency visible.
activities.rationale: Putting the property to work shows it reduces fact load and makes calculation easier, linking commutativity to fluency rather than leaving it as an abstract statement.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3: apply properties of operations as strategies, including the commutative property of addition.
learnerActions: Given 3+8, decide which number to start from so there is less counting on to do, and explain your choice.
Count on from the larger addend to reach the total, then check against counting on from the smaller to confirm they agree.
Try 2+9: say which order you would count on from and why.
State the matching fact instantly: if you know 8+3, say 3+8 without recounting.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order does not change an addition total, you can always start from the larger number and count on the smaller one, which takes fewer steps (unless the two numbers are equal, as in 6+6) — commutativity is a calculation-saving strategy, and knowing one fact gives you its partner.

activities.title: Convince me: why addition swaps but subtraction doesn't
feedback: If the child claims 8−5 = 5−8: have them physically attempt to take 8 from a pile of 5 — it cannot be done — and name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
If the justification is 'because that's the rule': ask for a drawing or counter arrangement that shows the whole staying the same.
activities.rationale: The objective includes justifying why addition commutes but subtraction does not; prompting the child to explain and to test the claim on subtraction develops that reasoning directly through the structural contrast.
sourceClaims: Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Argue why 3+8 must equal 8+3, using a drawing or a rearrangement of objects rather than just asserting the rule.
Test whether the same swap works for take-away: predict, then model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters and report what happens.
Consider 6+6: does order matter here, and what does that tell you about the rule?
State in your own words which operation can be reordered and why the other cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them, so the whole is unchanged; subtraction removes one amount from another, so swapping changes the starting amount and the result. Justifying this builds reasoning beyond recall.

activities.title: True/false and matching checks
feedback: If a subtraction pair is marked true: return to counters to show the results differ (5−3 = 2, but with 3 counters you run out and cannot take 5 away).
If the child cannot pick the efficient order: compare the number of count-on steps for each option.
activities.rationale: True/false, matching and strategy-choice items assess the property and the non-commutativity of subtraction. These recognition items check understanding but do not on their own elicit the child rearranging quantities or justifying; pair them with the swap and justification activities.
learnerActions: Decide whether statements are true or false: is 3+8 = 8+3? is 5−3 = 3−5?
Match each addition to its swapped partner that gives the same total.
Choose which order is easier to count on from for a given sum, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition statements hold when the order is swapped; subtraction statements do not. Recognising this consolidates the distinction and the strategic use of counting on from the larger number.

constraints: Show commutativity structurally — the same quantity rearranged — not as a rule to memorise.
Always include the subtraction contrast (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5); omitting it risks children over-generalising 'you can swap them'.
Watch for word-problem contexts where order encodes meaning (start/change); 'swap them' should not be applied there.

Recognition-only items (true/false, matching, multiple choice) assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the child independently rearranging quantities or justifying; use them alongside construction and explanation tasks.

A static side-by-side of 3+8 and 8+3 with the same objects can anchor the property, but it does not let the child perform the swap and watch the total hold; treat it as a scaffold toward hands-on or responsive work.
When demonstrating 5−8 or 3−5 with young children, frame it as 'you run out / cannot take that many away' rather than introducing negative numbers as a target concept.
When contrasting a subtraction pair, keep the two numbers consistent across the action and its feedback (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5), so the 'you run out' example matches the pair the child is working with.

The original labelled a live invariance-vs-change contrast as 'impossible statically' and said 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit claims, not established necessity. They have been softened to scoped affordances (a static image cannot be manipulated but can still anchor the property).

Of the three cited sources, two are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.3 and the NCETM mastery claim); only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Treat citation strength accordingly.

The assessment's probe '5 − 8' and 'take 5 cubes and try to remove 8' edges toward negative numbers; for ages 6-7 this is best handled as 'cannot be done / goes below what you have' rather than teaching negatives, which has been reflected in the constraints.

Independent re-audit confirmed Activity 1's subtraction feedback now matches its stated 5−3/3−5 pair ('3 cannot have 5 removed'), Activity 3 consistently uses the 8−5/5−8 pair, and all arithmetic (3+8=8+3=11, 2+9, 5−3=2, 8−5=3) is correct; no remaining internal contradictions or unsupported categorical modality claims were found.

probeDeeper: Why does swapping the two numbers not change the total in an addition?
You said 8 − 5 isn't the same as 5 − 8 — show me with counters why not.
What about 6 + 6 — does order matter there? What does that tell you about the rule?
For 2 + 9, which order would you choose to count on from, and why?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can do any sum in any order' — over-applies commutativity to subtraction, claiming 5 − 8 = 8 − 5 = 3.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters — you cannot take 8 from a pile of 5; order matters. Name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: asserts subtraction gives the same answer whichever way round.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'd better count it again' — does not trust that swapping preserves the total, so recomputes 5 + 8 from one instead of using the known fact.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show both orders built on the SAME set of counters or the same bar; the total is one unchanging quantity. Practise stating the swapped fact instantly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts all / counts on from scratch rather than stating 13 immediately.

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes both additions and/or thinks order changes an addition total, or claims subtraction is commutative.
responseLevels.full: States the addition total is unchanged because the same amounts are combined, uses commutativity to count on from the larger addend, AND correctly denies that subtraction is commutative, justifying with counters.
responseLevels.partial: Knows addition works in any order and uses it to count on from the larger, but over-generalises to subtraction OR cannot explain why the total is unchanged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 + 5 = 13. So what is 5 + 8? And does the same trick work for taking away — do 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 give the same answer? Tell me why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child running a shallow 'any order works' rule gives the addition right AND wrongly says 8−5 = 5−8; a child who understands commutativity as 'the same quantities combined' restricts it to addition and rejects it for subtraction. The addition half is easy for everyone — the subtraction contrast is what separates real understanding from an over-applied slogan.

topic.name: Fluent addition and subtraction
topic.description: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
evidence: Rapidly recall 7 + 8 = 15 and 15 − 8 = 7
Use 6 + 4 = 10 to derive 60 + 40 = 100
Derive 35 + 5 = 40 from knowledge that 5 + 5 = 10
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '9 + 7 = 16' and '16 − 7 = 9', and use those to help work out bigger sums like '90 + 70'?

pedagogy.summary: This topic has two linked strands: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds (6+4=10 → 60+40=100; 5+5=10 → 35+5=40). Recall is built from secure make-ten strategy plus spaced retrieval, not speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units, so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.
bestPractices: Build automaticity from strategy, then retrieval: secure make-ten within 20 first, then space low-stakes recall practice so facts move to memory (DfE: emphasis on practice aids fluency)
Teach fact families so + and − are learned together (7+8=15, 15−8=7, 15−7=8) and the inverse is available
Derive decade facts by scaling a known bond: 6+4=10 becomes 60+40=100 because six tens plus four tens is ten tens
Use the same visual at two scales (ten-frame counters vs ten-rods) to show 6+4 and 60+40 are one picture
Avoid timed pressure that induces anxiety; keep finger/strategy use welcome while retrieval matures
keyRepresentations: Ten-frame / double ten-frame (make-ten)
Fact-family triangle (shows the three related facts)
Bead string / Rekenrek
Base-ten ten-rods (scaling a bond to tens)
Number bonds part-whole diagram
commonMisconceptions: Recall not automatic — still counting on fingers every time for 7+8
Failing to scale the bond: knowing 6+4=10 but giving 60+40=10 or 70 or 700
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so 15−8 is re-counted despite knowing 7+8=15
Applying a derived pattern blindly (e.g. 35+5=40 but then 35+50=40)

learn.summary: Two linked goals for ages 6–7: automatic recall of addition and subtraction facts to 20 (so 7+8 and 15−8 come without calculating) and derivation of related facts to 100 by scaling and using known bonds — 6+4=10 → 60+40=100 by scaling the bond to tens, and 5+5=10 → 35+5=40 by using the ones bond inside a larger number. Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval rather than speed drills; derivation is built by treating tens as units so a known bond reappears at a larger scale.

activities.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40
feedback: If a child gives 60+40=10, 70 or 700, show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods) and name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100.
If a child says 35+50=40, slow down and count the tens being added: adding five tens to 35 gives 85, while adding five ones gives 40. Keep both comparisons visible side by side.
When a child derives correctly, ask 'how did you know that?' so the scaling or ones-bond reasoning is spoken, not just the answer.
activities.rationale: Using the same visual at two scales makes 'derive' concrete: a known within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens by unitising. A manipulable or scalable model lets the learner see the identical make-ten action produce 10 and then 100; a fixed two-scale picture can also show this relationship.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.

activities.title: Fact-family triangle: one trio, both operations
feedback: If a child re-counts 15−8 straight after giving 7+8=15, lay out the fact family 7, 8, 15 and show the same three numbers make both facts.
Prompt: 'If 7+8=15, what subtraction facts do you already know without working them out?'
A tap-to-reveal triangle is good reference for the inverse link but does not by itself build recall speed; pair it with retrieval practice.
activities.rationale: Teaching fact families makes the inverse explicit so + and − are learned together and the inverse is immediately available. This supports the misconception where subtraction is treated as a separate unknown fact.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
learnerActions: Lay out the three numbers 7, 8 and 15 on a fact-family triangle (part–part–whole).
Cover one corner and read off the fact it reveals: cover 15 to get 7+8=15 and 8+7=15; cover 7 to get 15−8=7; cover 8 to get 15−7=8.
State explicitly: because 7+8=15, you already know 15−8 and 15−7 without re-counting.
Build a second family (e.g. 6, 9, 15, giving 6+9=15, 9+6=15, 15−6=9, 15−9=6) and name all its related facts the same way.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition and subtraction are the same relationship between three numbers; knowing one fact hands you the inverse, so 15−8 need not be re-counted once 7+8=15 is known.

activities.title: Spaced, untimed retrieval to build automatic recall
feedback: If a child counts on fingers for 7+8 every time with no drop in effort on a second asking, do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — keep practising the make-ten strategy and spaced recall without the clock.
For a derive prompt like '6+4=10, so 60+40=?', if a wrong value such as 10, 70 or 700 is chosen, return to the two-scale picture and re-establish six tens plus four tens = 100.
Ask 'which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?' to make the recall/calculation distinction visible to the learner.
activities.rationale: Recall is built from a secure make-ten strategy then moved to memory by spaced low-stakes practice; timed pressure can induce anxiety and is avoided. A self-paced fill-in or choice format can exercise retrieval and check the derive insight, but repeated spaced practice, not a single check, is what builds automaticity.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive and use related facts up to 100 (e.g. 3+7=10 → 30+70=100); an emphasis on practice at this stage aids fluency, and knowing number bonds establishes addition and subtraction as related operations.
Recall of pairs that make ten supports calculation, and known facts are extended by unitising tens so a within-ten bond is reused at the scale of tens.
learnerActions: Practise recalling facts to 20 in short, low-stakes sessions spread over days (e.g. 7+8, 15−8, 6+4, 9+4), rather than one long timed drill.
Mix in derive-a-fact prompts such as '6+4=10, so 60+40=?' and '5+5=10, so 35+5=?', choosing or writing the answer.
After each prompt, say which ones you just knew and which you had to work out.
Keep finger and make-ten strategy use welcome; the aim is that repeated facts need less effort each time, not beating a clock.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity grows from secure strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval; a fact becomes 'known' when recalling it needs noticeably less effort on later encounters.

activities.title: Playful recall talk: 'how did you know that?'
feedback: Spoken back-and-forth gives retrieval practice but does not by itself build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight; pair it with the ten-frame and two-scale work.
If a child cannot explain how they knew a fact, return to the relevant model (ten-frame or fact-family triangle) before more recall practice.
activities.rationale: A conversational recall routine offers extra retrieval opportunities and surfaces thinking, complementing the manipulative and the fact-family work without replacing the strategy-building they provide.
learnerActions: Trade quick spoken recall prompts back and forth with a partner or adult (flashcard-style), e.g. one asks 7+8, then 15−8, then 6+4.
For each answer, the asker follows up with 'how did you know that?' — did you just know it, make ten, or use the inverse?
Keep it low-stakes and untimed; celebrate strategy explanations as much as correct answers.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising recall and the reasoning behind it reinforces both the facts and the strategies (make-ten, inverse, scaling) that generate them.

constraints: Do not use timed drills or penalise finger/strategy use; automaticity is to grow from a secure make-ten strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval.

A tap-to-reveal fact-family triangle is a reference scaffold for the inverse relationship; it does not exercise retrieval speed or the scaling derivation, so pair it with practice and the two-scale model.
A fill-in or choice retrieval format can check the derive insight and give recall practice, but a single check does not build automaticity; genuine fluency needs repeated spaced practice over time.
Recognition/choice responses alone do not elicit independent construction of a derived fact; include prompts where the child states or writes the answer and explains the scaling.
A conversational recall routine is a supplementary retrieval vehicle; it does not directly build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight.

Keep the ones-vs-tens distinction explicit (35+5=40 by adding five ones vs 35+50=85 by adding five tens) so the derived pattern is not applied blindly, and keep scaling to tens (60+40) distinct from using a ones bond inside a number (35+5).

The legacy framing that a scalable tool 'turns derive into it's the same fact' overstates necessity; a fixed two-scale picture can also show the relationship, so the activity keeps the model affordance without claiming one medium is uniquely required.
The original bead string / Rekenrek representation was not carried into these activities; it remains a valid make-ten manipulative if an implementer wishes to add it.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Grouping numbers to add
topic.description: Understand and apply the associative property of addition: when adding three numbers, any two can be added first
evidence: Solve 2 + 6 + 4 by first adding 6 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 10 = 12
Explain that grouping addends differently gives the same total
Choose which two numbers to add first to make the calculation easier
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3 + 7 + 6, can they spot that adding 3 and 7 first (to make 10) is easier — rather than always working left to right?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Associative property of addition — when adding three or more numbers, they may be grouped (added) in any order without changing the total, e.g. (2+3)+5 = 2+(3+5). For ages 6–7, layered on commutativity and used as a strategy tool, not a stated law.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 pupils 'show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of one number from another cannot'; associative grouping underpins Y2 'add numbers using... a three-digit number and ones/tens' and the Y3 formal written methods where partial sums are recombined. Named explicitly as a mental strategy in KS2 guidance.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract... To add 2+6+4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 (Associative property of addition).' Children need not use formal terms.
• Operational details: teach as a licence to regroup for convenience — look-for-a-ten, add doubles first, add the friendly pair. Contrast with commutativity (reorder) — association is about which pair you combine FIRST. Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities are unchanged, only the sequence of combining differs.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — given 2+8+5, child chooses to add 2+8 to make 10 first and explains why that is allowed. Tier B (age 7) — regroups three addends two different ways and confirms the same total. Tier C (age 7+) — uses grouping to justify a mental strategy in a worded context and states that regrouping never changes the sum.
bestPractices: Introduce through the practical goal of making calculation easier (look for a pair that makes ten, or add a double first) rather than as an abstract named law.
Use concrete equal-status objects (counters, cubes) the child physically pushes into different pairs, so the conserved whole is seen while the grouping order varies.
Contrast explicitly with commutativity: reordering (which comes first) versus associating (which pair we combine first) — pupils confuse the two.
Have children compute the same triple by two different groupings and compare totals, making the invariance an observed result, not a told fact.
Connect forward to written column addition, where partial sums (ones, tens) are grouped and recombined, so the property is seen as load-bearing later.
keyRepresentations: Three counter groups / cube towers that can be pushed into different pairs before merging
Bracket notation over three addends, (a+b)+c vs a+(b+c), with the first-combined pair highlighted
Ten-frame showing a make-ten pair filling first, then the remainder added
Bar/part-whole model with three parts and one conserved whole bar
Empty number line where the child chooses which jump to take first
commonMisconceptions: Believing the total changes if you add in a different grouping (failing to conserve the whole).
Conflating associativity with commutativity — thinking they are the same 'any order' rule.
Over-generalising to subtraction, e.g. assuming (10−3)−2 = 10−(3−2).
Losing track of an addend when regrouping (dropping or double-counting the third number).
Thinking brackets are just decoration rather than an instruction about what to combine first.

learn.summary: Teaches the associative property of addition for ages 6–7: when adding three or more numbers, any two can be combined first without changing the total, e.g. (2+8)+5 = 2+(8+5) = 15. The point is the freedom to choose which pair to combine first, used as a practical strategy (make a ten, add a double first) rather than as a stated law. Contrast with commutativity (reordering the numbers) and avoid over-generalising to subtraction, where (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9. Includes hands-on manipulation, a reasoning/justification layer, consolidation checks, and a static side-by-side anchor, each with its pedagogical purpose and limits noted.

activities.title: Grouping bench: choose which pair to combine first
feedback: If a learner reaches the same total both ways, name the move: 'You grouped these two first — that's allowed, and the total stayed the same.'
If a learner expects the total to change under a different grouping, have them compute both groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
If a learner loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten, physically set the third object aside and bring it in last, then recount — this is a tracking slip, not a concept error.
When a make-ten pair is chosen, point out how the second step (e.g. 10+5) became easy.
activities.rationale: The concept is the freedom to decide which pair to combine first, so letting the learner physically make and compare that choice is intended to turn invariance into an observed result rather than a told fact, and to surface WHY grouping helps. Standards frame this as a strategy, not a named law.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
Making ten by regrouping addends is a key mental calculation strategy in early KS1/KS2.
Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
learnerActions: Set out three equal-status objects or number tiles for a triple such as 2, 8, 5 (counters, cubes, or draggable tiles).
Choose any two to combine first; merge them into a single running sum, then bring in the third.
Try the same triple a second way (e.g. combine 8+5 first) and compare the final total.
State out loud which pair you combined first and why that choice made the calculation easier.
Repeat with a triple that rewards a make-ten pair (e.g. 2+8+5, where 2+8=10 then 10+5=15) and one that rewards adding a double first (e.g. 4+4+7, where 4+4=8 then 8+7=15).
activities.intendedInsight: You may choose which pair to combine first; a smart choice (make a ten, or add a double) makes the sum easier while the total stays identical because the three amounts themselves never change.

activities.title: Why is that allowed? Justify your grouping
feedback: If the learner justifies by pointing to the unchanged amounts, name that reasoning back as 'grouping'.
If the learner cannot say why the total is the same, return to combining the same triple two ways and comparing before asking again.
Probe with 'what's your evidence the total is still the same if you group differently?' to move from a one-off trick toward a general reason.

If a learner tries the subtraction pair, confirm (10−3)−2 = 5 but 10−(3−2) = 9 — the answers differ, so subtraction cannot be regrouped the way addition can; use this only as a contrast, never as a rule to apply.
activities.rationale: Early standards ask pupils to show/apply the property and explain their strategy, so an explain/justify layer is intended to develop the reasoning the numeric answer alone does not reveal; the subtraction contrast targets the common over-generalisation.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show addition can be done in any order and use this alongside grouping when adding a three-digit number and ones/tens; formal written methods recombine partial sums.
1.OA.3 applies properties of operations as strategies, giving the associative example 2+6+4 = 2+10 = 12 and noting children need not use formal terms.
learnerActions: Given a triple, say which two numbers you would add first.
Answer a questioner (a peer, tutor, or 'maths buddy') who asks 'Why is that allowed?' and 'Would we get the same total if we grouped the numbers differently? How do you know?'
Explain in your own words that the three amounts are unchanged, so only which pair you combine first differs.

Try a new triple such as 4+7+6 and justify which pair you would add first (here 4+6=10, then 10+7=17). Notice that 4 and 6 are not next to each other, so adding them first means changing the order as well as the grouping; the total is still 17.
Test the contrast with subtraction: work out (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, notice the answers differ, and conclude that the grouping freedom belongs to addition, not subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: Grouping is a reasoning move you can justify: the total is conserved because the three quantities stay the same, no matter which pair you combine first — but this freedom holds for addition, not for subtraction.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, choose, and check equal totals
feedback: For the efficient-pair item, confirm the make-ten pair and show the easy second step.
For a true/false item where a number was altered, point out that the total changed because an amount changed, not because of regrouping.
activities.rationale: Closed-response items are intended to consolidate recognition of equivalent groupings after hands-on work; whether they do so is not established here. This is a check/consolidation step; it does not by itself let a learner freely explore their own alternative groupings, and recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own production of a grouping.
learnerActions: Decide which pair you would add first to make a given triple easy (e.g. for 2+8+5, which pair makes a ten?).
Match equivalent groupings, e.g. (2+8)+5 with 2+(8+5).
Judge true/false statements about whether two groupings of the same triple share a total, including an item where one number has been changed so the total genuinely differs.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising equivalent groupings and spotting the efficient first pair is intended to consolidate that regrouping preserves the total while making the calculation easier.

activities.title: Side-by-side anchor: did the total change?
feedback: Confirm that the brackets changed which pair came first but the final total stayed the same.
If a learner treats brackets as decoration, point to the highlighted first pair and the matching final totals.
activities.rationale: A fixed side-by-side display is a clear reference anchor for the bracket-reading idea. It is a scaffold: because the triples are pre-set, it cannot let the learner test their own choice of grouping, which is the heart of the property.
learnerActions: Look at two pre-set groupings of the same triple, e.g. (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5), with brackets marking each first pair.
Reveal each intermediate sum and the shared final total (both land on 15).
Answer 'Did the total change?' and explain what the brackets tell you to combine first.
activities.intendedInsight: Brackets are an instruction about what to combine first, not decoration, and both groupings reach the same total.

constraints: Teach as a licence to regroup for convenience (look for a ten, add a double first), not as an abstract named law; children need not use the formal term 'associative'.

Distinguish associativity (which pair we combine FIRST) from commutativity (which order numbers come in); learners frequently conflate them, so address them explicitly. Note that combining two numbers that are not next to each other first (e.g. 4 and 6 in 4+7+6, or 2 and 5 in 2+8+5) uses both properties together.
Do NOT extend the grouping rule to subtraction: (10−3)−2 = 5 does not equal 10−(3−2) = 9. Use this contrast to probe, not as a rule to apply.
Keep the whole conserved: the three quantities stay the same; only which pair is combined first differs. Guard against dropping or double-counting an addend during regrouping.

Closed matching/true-false items and the fixed side-by-side anchor are consolidation and reference scaffolds; they do not let a learner freely explore alternative groupings and should follow, not replace, hands-on choice. This is an observable limit of those formats, not a claim that only manipulation can teach the concept.

The optional interactive touches (a total bar pinned at a fixed value while intermediate sums recompute, a make-ten pair glowing, tiles fusing on drag) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.

Self-audit arithmetic: 2+8+5=15 and 2+6+4=12 are correct in both groupings; 4+4+7=15; 4+7+6=17. The deliberately altered true/false distractor should change a number so the total genuinely differs — do not present two correct groupings as giving different totals.
Subtraction check: (10−3)−2 = 5 and 10−(3−2) = 9, so subtraction is NOT associative; this is used only as a contrast/probe in the justify activity, never taught as working.
Source note: the CCSS-M claim and the NCETM claim are marked verified:false in the row; the DfE claim is marked verified:true. Confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

The original 3D-interactive entry was judged a poor fit with the boilerplate reasoning 'a flat concept is not made 3D by rendering it in 3D'; this universal-sounding claim is not established by the source material and was dropped rather than propagated as a law.
The forward connection to column addition (recombining partial sums) is carried only in standards framing, not as its own activity; a follow-on activity could make that link explicit.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether adding (2 + 8) first or (8 + 5) first changes the answer to 2 + 8 + 5. Say your prediction and why. Then work out both ways and check — what does the result tell you about grouping?
probeDeeper: Why did you choose those two numbers to add first?
What's your evidence the total is still 15 if you group the numbers differently?
What if the numbers were 4 + 7 + 6 — which pair would you add first, and why?
Does this grouping trick work for subtraction? Try (10 − 3) − 2 and 10 − (3 − 2) and see.
assess.correctAnswer: 15. A strong answer adds 2 + 8 to make 10 first, then 10 + 5 = 15, choosing that pair because it makes a ten. The total is 15 whatever grouping is used — the three amounts don't change, only which pair is combined first.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — adds strictly left-to-right and resists regrouping to make a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build (2+8)+5 and 2+(8+5) with cubes side by side; both reach 15. Establish that you may choose any pair to combine first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on 2+8 then +5 only because that is the written order; will not try 8+5 or 2+... to make ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a different grouping changes the total.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute two groupings of the same triple side by side and compare the equal totals; stress the amounts are unchanged.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — grouping them differently would give a different total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a different answer if the numbers are grouped another way.

errorPatterns.pattern: Loses or double-counts the third addend after making a ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count.

responseLevels.full: Explains the total is conserved under any grouping because the three amounts are unchanged, and deliberately chooses a make-ten pair to make the calculation easier.
responseLevels.partial: Can add the three and may even use make-ten, but cannot explain why any grouping gives the same total, or treats it as a one-off trick for this case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work out 2 + 8 + 5. Which two numbers did you add first, and why did you pick those? Would you get a different total if you added them in a different order?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child adding mechanically left-to-right can still reach 15, so the numeric answer alone doesn't discriminate. The 'which did you add first / would a different order change it' tier reveals whether the child sees grouping as a free, total-preserving choice (and spots the make-ten pair) or believes the written order is fixed / that regrouping changes the total.
